pages.title: Substitute vs. Outcome Model of Dividends
pages.excerpt: The substitute-versus-outcome debate concerns the causal relationship between the legal protection of minority shareholders and corporate dividend payouts, framed as two rival agency models of why firms distribute cash. Both models begin from the same premise — that a dividend…
pages.text: Substitute vs. Outcome Model of Dividends The substitute-versus-outcome debate concerns the causal relationship between the legal protection of minority shareholders and corporate dividend payouts, framed as two rival agency models of why firms distribute cash. Both models begin from the same premise — that a dividend is an agency cost paid to align the interests of insiders and outside investors — yet they reach diametrically opposed conclusions. In the outcome model, dividends are an outcome of strong shareholder rights: empowered minority investors use their legal leverage to force insiders to disgorge cash, so stronger protection predicts higher payouts. In the substitute model, dividends are a substitute for weak protection: insiders who anticipate returning to capital markets pay dividends voluntarily to build a reputation for decent treatment, so stronger protection predicts lower payouts. Because the two models generate opposite-signed predictions about the same protection–payout correlation, the axis is a genuine debate rather than a pair of complementary claims, and it has organised the entire law-and-finance strand of the payout literature. This page treats the debate framing itself — the two models and their conflicting predictions; the empirical relationship is adjudicated in investor-protection-and-payout and the underlying institutional construct is defined in investor-protection. The question Both models take as given that separating ownership from control creates an agency problem: insiders control corporate cash and may divert it to private benefits rather than return it to dispersed outside investors. A dividend, in this framing, is a device that transfers cash out of insider control, and the question is what makes insiders part with it. The founding treatment, La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny's cross-country study, poses the question in explicitly institutional terms and answers it against a 33-country cross-section, making legal protection of minority shareholders the variable whose variation identifies the mechanism (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). This design is inseparable from the broader legal-origins research program, in which cross-country differences in ownership concentration, capital-market depth, and payout all trace back to how well law shields investors from expropriation by managers and controlling shareholders (laporta-2000-investor-protection-and-corporate-governance). The distinctive difficulty is that the shared agency premise does not pin down the sign: the same logic of dividends-as-agency-cost supports either that protection causes payouts (by empowering the demanders) or that weak protection induces them (by making voluntary bonding worthwhile). A laboratory experiment reframes the question as a clean causal one — what does exogenously strengthening protection do to payouts, expropriation, and investment simultaneously — precisely because archival cross-sections cannot isolate the direction (lariviere-2018-shareholder-protection-and-agency-costs-an-experimental-analysis). The outcome model The outcome model reads dividends as the product of shareholder power. Where minority investors enjoy strong legal rights — the ability to vote out directors, sue for oppression, or block self-dealing — they can pressure insiders to pay out free cash rather than let it fund empire-building or be diverted. The prediction is a positive protection–payout relationship: stronger rights, higher payouts. The founding cross-section of roughly 4,000 firms across 33 countries supports precisely this model, finding that firms in better-protected legal environments pay more (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). The empirical signature is not merely a level correlation but a change prediction: payouts should rise when governance strengthens, and the rise should concentrate in firms that were previously most vulnerable to insider entrenchment. Board reforms enacted across 40 countries provide the cleanest test — a difference-in-differences design finds firms pay higher dividends after reform, with the increase most pronounced for firms with weak pre-reform board governance and in countries with strong external governance (bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence). At the micro level, minority shareholders' voting opposition to dividend proposals on the Shanghai exchange predicts significantly higher payouts the following year, and reduces expropriation by major shareholders, supplying a granular mechanism for the empowered-demander channel (lin-2023-minority-shareholder-voting-and-dividend-policy). Cross-paper pattern: The LLSV cross-section and the 40-country board-reform difference-in-differences converge on the outcome prediction from two different research designs — one exploiting cross-country institutional variation, the other a within-country regulatory shock — with the effect concentrated in exactly the weakly-governed firms the model predicts (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence; lin-2023-minority-shareholder-voting-and-dividend-policy). A boundary case complicates the naive reading. Among Delaware master limited partnerships, weaker governance is associated with higher cash payouts that destroy firm value — consistent not with empowered minorities extracting cash but with the general partner tunneling resources out at the expense of limited unitholders (atanassov-2018-corporate-governance-and-dividend-policy-evidence-of-tunneling). High payouts, in other words, are not always a sign that the outcome mechanism is working; the same observable can mask extraction. The substitute model The substitute model inverts the causal arrow. Where legal protection is weak, insiders who intend to raise external equity in the future have a private incentive to establish a reputation for treating minority shareholders decently, and a costly, visible, repeated commitment — paying large and stable dividends — is the bonding device that builds it. The prediction is a negative protection–payout relationship: the weaker the law, the greater the need to substitute a voluntary reputational commitment, and the higher the payout. The founding paper names this model and states its opposite-signed prediction explicitly, even though its own cross-section does not favour it (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). Shock-based studies supply the model's strongest empirical support. Firms in countries with weak insider-trading laws exhibit a higher propensity to pay, larger dividend amounts, and greater dividend smoothing, and the market values those dividends more highly — a pattern the authors interpret as dividends serving as a substitute bonding mechanism where legal protection fails (brockman-2014-the-impact-of-insider-trading-laws-on-dividend). The empirical signature is therefore multidimensional: not just higher payout levels but greater smoothing and higher dividend valuation where protection is weakest. Two further regulatory-shock studies reinforce the substitute logic by showing payouts fall when protection or its functional equivalents strengthen. The staggered initiation of country-level M&A laws — which raises the threat of takeover and thereby the market's disciplinary pressure on managers — significantly reduces both the likelihood and the amount of dividends across 34 countries, because a credible takeover market lowers the need to signal commitment through costly payouts (glendening-2016-the-market-for-corporate-control-and-dividend-policies). Similarly, mandatory IFRS adoption and initial insider-trading-law enforcement, both of which improve the public information environment, make firms less likely to pay or increase dividends and more likely to cut them, as better information reduces managers' need to bond via payout (hail-2014-dividend-payouts-and-information-shocks). Where they actually disagree The disagreement is sharp and can be stated as a sign flip on a single coefficient. Let $\rho$ denote the correlation between the strength of minority-shareholder protection and dividend payout. The outcome model predicts $\rho > 0$; the substitute model predicts $\rho < 0$. The models differ on three linked dimensions. First, on sign: whether stronger rights raise or lower payouts. Second, on the direction of causation: the outcome model runs protection → minority leverage → forced disgorgement, whereas the substitute model runs weak protection → insiders' anticipated financing need → voluntary payout. Third, on the binding motive: the outcome model makes extraction-prevention by empowered outsiders the operative force, the substitute model makes reputation-building by self-interested insiders the operative force. What the two share is the treatment of dividends as an agency cost that aligns insider and outsider interests — a point the experimental treatment makes explicit, noting that under either model the payout is a cost incurred to bridge the insider-investor divide (lariviere-2018-shareholder-protection-and-agency-costs-an-experimental-analysis; laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). Because they agree on the premise and disagree only on the sign, no single correlation can confirm one without disconfirming the other — which is why the reconciliation turns on scope conditions rather than a flat verdict (chae-2009-how-corporate-governance-affects-payout-policy-under-agency). Empirical anchors The decisive evidence spans three research designs pulling in partly different directions. The founding 33-country cross-section is the anchor for the outcome model: across roughly 4,000 firms, better minority protection is associated with higher payouts (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). The laboratory experiment is the anchor for causal identification, and its result is subtle: strengthening investor protection raises dividend payout ratios about fivefold, consistent with the outcome model, but it also raises insider expropriation roughly twofold and reduces outsider investment by about 45%, revealing agency costs that neither archival model had isolated (lariviere-2018-shareholder-protection-and-agency-costs-an-experimental-analysis). The shock-based studies are the anchors for the substitute model and for conditionality: board reforms raise payouts (bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence), while M&A-law and information shocks lower them (glendening-2016-the-market-for-corporate-control-and-dividend-policies; brockman-2014-the-impact-of-insider-trading-laws-on-dividend; hail-2014-dividend-payouts-and-information-shocks). The apparent contradiction — rigorous natural experiments producing opposite signs — is the empirical puzzle the debate must resolve, and it is what shifts attention from which model is right to when each holds. Reconciling the models: scope conditions The reconciliation hinges on recognising that the two models describe different margins that dominate under different conditions. The pivotal result comes from jointly modelling agency problems and external-financing constraints: firms with high external-financing constraints decrease payout as governance improves (the substitute margin — better governance lets them retain cash and avoid costly issuance), while firms with low constraints increase payout as governance improves (the outcome margin — empowered outsiders extract free cash). The sign of the governance–payout relation reverses depending on the relative magnitude of agency costs versus external-financing costs (chae-2009-how-corporate-governance-affects-payout-policy-under-agency). This contingency also rationalises the divergent shocks. Board reforms strengthen internal monitoring and empower outsiders to demand cash, so payouts rise (bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence); M&A laws substitute an external disciplinary mechanism — the takeover threat — for the payout commitment, so payouts fall (glendening-2016-the-market-for-corporate-control-and-dividend-policies); and information shocks lower the informational value of the payout commitment, so payouts also fall (hail-2014-dividend-payouts-and-information-shocks). Cross-paper pattern: The sign of the protection–payout relationship is not a fixed empirical fact but a function of two scope conditions — the firm's external-financing constraint relative to its agency costs, and whether the strengthened institution empowers demanders (board reform) or substitutes for the payout's disciplinary role (takeover threat, better information) (chae-2009-how-corporate-governance-affects-payout-policy-under-agency; glendening-2016-the-market-for-corporate-control-and-dividend-policies; hail-2014-dividend-payouts-and-information-shocks; bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence). Current state of the debate The modal empirical verdict favours the outcome model — the founding cross-section, the board-reform shock, and the causal direction of the laboratory experiment all point to protection raising payouts (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; bae-2021-board-reforms-and-dividend-policy-international-evidence; lariviere-2018-shareholder-protection-and-agency-costs-an-experimental-analysis). But the substitute logic has not been refuted; it survives as a scope-conditional bonding channel that dominates where firms face binding external-financing constraints or where a strengthened institution displaces rather than empowers the payout commitment (chae-2009-how-corporate-governance-affects-payout-policy-under-agency). Open questions concern mechanism substitution — how takeover threat, information environment, and legal rights trade off as alternative disciplinary devices — and heterogeneity in which margin binds for which firms. Current assessment (2026-07): The debate is best read not as "which model wins" but as "which margin dominates when." The outcome model is the modal verdict for the level relationship and for clean empowerment shocks; the substitute model holds where financing constraints bind or where a strengthened institution substitutes for the dividend's disciplinary role. The experimental finding that stronger protection simultaneously raises payouts, expropriation, and disinvestment is the sharpest reminder that a higher payout is not, by itself, evidence that outsiders are better off. pages.title: Lintner Model and Smoothing Measures
pages.excerpt: The Lintner model is the canonical partial-adjustment specification used to describe and quantify how firms set dividends, and it anchors the family of smoothing measures derived from it. Lintner (1956) posited that a firm forms a target dividend as a payout ratio applied to…
pages.text: Lintner Model and Smoothing Measures The Lintner model is the canonical partial-adjustment specification used to describe and quantify how firms set dividends, and it anchors the family of smoothing measures derived from it. Lintner (1956) posited that a firm forms a target dividend as a payout ratio applied to earnings and then closes only a fraction of the gap between that target and last period's dividend each year; the fraction closed is the speed of adjustment, and its complement is the standard scalar index of smoothing, so a low speed of adjustment means stickier, more heavily smoothed dividends. This apparatus matters because almost every empirical claim about smoothing is mediated by it: the estimated speed of adjustment is the number researchers regress on firm and country characteristics, extend from dividends to total payout, or blame for confounding signaling and predictability tests. This page documents what the model measures, its estimating equation, how the speed of adjustment and related indices are computed and validated, the main variants — total-payout Lintner models, structural estimation, and dynamic-model measures — and the known biases that complicate comparison across studies. The substantive economics of why firms smooth is treated on the companion concept page dividend-smoothing; this page is the "how measured" counterpart. What is being measured The object of measurement is the responsiveness of dividends to earnings: a smoothing firm adjusts its dividend slowly and keeps the current dividend relatively insensitive to current earnings, whereas a non-smoothing firm passes earnings through more fully. Operationally, smoothing is captured as slow adjustment toward a target payout — a strong loading on the lagged dividend and a weak loading on current earnings (aivazian-2006-dividend-smoothing-and-debt-ratings; leary-2011-determinants-of-dividend-smoothing-empirical-evidence). The measure presupposes a well-defined target payout ratio, and a first-order choice is what payout it applies to. When the target is defined over regular dividends alone, the measure describes dividend stickiness; when it is defined over total payout (dividends plus net repurchases), it describes the smoothness of the whole distribution stream, and the two need not coincide once repurchases and special dividends are available (andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts; lambrecht-2012-a-lintner-model-of-payout-and-managerial-rents). Because the quantity being estimated is a behavioral parameter rather than an accounting ratio, the same firm can look smoothing or residual depending on which payout definition and which sample the researcher adopts, which is why the measure's construction is inseparable from the substantive conclusions drawn from it. Formal model Lintner's specification begins with a target dividend proportional to current earnings, $$D_t^{} = r\,E_t,$$ where $E_t$ is earnings in period $t$, $D_t^{}$ is the target dividend, and $r$ is the target payout ratio. Firms do not jump to the target; they close only a fraction of the gap between the target and the previous dividend: $$\Delta D_t = \alpha + c\,\bigl(D_t^{} - D{t-1}\bigr) + \varepsilon_t,$$ where $\Delta D_t = D_t - D{t-1}$ is the dividend change, $\alpha$ is a drift term capturing managers' reluctance to cut, $c \in (0,1]$ is the speed of adjustment (SOA), and $\varepsilon_t$ is a disturbance. The scalar smoothing index is the complement of the speed of adjustment, $(1-c)$: a value near one denotes heavy smoothing, a value near zero a near-residual policy. Substituting the target gives the estimating reduced form in the lagged dividend and current earnings, $$D_t = \alpha + (1-c)\,D{t-1} + c\,r\,E_t + \varepsilon_t,$$ so a regression of the current dividend on its own lag and current earnings recovers $(1-c)$ as the coefficient on $D{t-1}$ and $c\,r$ as the coefficient on $E_t$; the target ratio is backed out as $r = (\text{earnings coefficient})/c$. A smoothing firm shows a large lagged-dividend coefficient and a small earnings coefficient. This target-adjustment form is not merely descriptive: lambrecht-2012-a-lintner-model-of-payout-and-managerial-rents microfound it for total payout in a dynamic agency model, deriving the result that payout absorbs transitory income shocks and adjusts only gradually to permanent-income changes — exactly the partial-adjustment behavior Lintner assumed — with smoothing achieved through borrowing and lending. Estimating the same partial-adjustment equation for both dividends and total payout is the empirical strategy of andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts. Estimation and validation In practice the reduced form is estimated firm-by-firm or in panels, and the recovered speed of adjustment is treated as the firm's smoothing measure. The measure is validated by its ability to sort firms into recognizable behavioral types: a "Lintner-style" firm exhibits a strong lagged-dividend loading and a weak current-earnings loading, while a residual-policy firm shows the reverse, flowing earnings straight through. The cleanest such validation comes from aivazian-2006-dividend-smoothing-and-debt-ratings, who show that firms with bond ratings follow the traditional Lintner pattern — prior dividend very influential, current dividend relatively insensitive to current earnings — whereas firms without bond ratings pass earnings through and display little smoothing, a near-residual policy. The measure also varies coherently with firm characteristics in the U.S. cross-section, smoothing more for mature cash cows and less for young, volatile, low-yield firms (leary-2011-determinants-of-dividend-smoothing-empirical-evidence), and it travels internationally, with the speed of adjustment estimated across more than two thousand firms in twenty-four countries and related to legal protection, culture, and tax regime (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). Explicit Lintner-model tests also detect cross-market differences, showing that Hong Kong firms adjust faster — smooth less — than U.S. firms (chemmanur-2010-is-dividend-smoothing-universal-new-insights-from-a). The empirical signature to look for is thus a diagnostic loading pattern rather than a single threshold: the lagged-dividend-versus-earnings coefficient split is what distinguishes smoothers from residual payers. Cross-paper pattern: A recurring split validates the measure across settings — bond-rated, large, mature firms load on the lagged dividend and smooth heavily, while unrated, smaller, or emerging-market firms flow earnings through in a near-residual policy (aivazian-2006-dividend-smoothing-and-debt-ratings; leary-2011-determinants-of-dividend-smoothing-empirical-evidence; chemmanur-2010-is-dividend-smoothing-universal-new-insights-from-a; javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). That the same estimated parameter separates these groups consistently is the main evidence that the speed of adjustment measures something real. Variants: dividends versus total payout The most consequential variant extends the partial-adjustment model from regular dividends to total payout, motivated by the rise of repurchases. andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts estimate Lintner partial-adjustment models for both dividends and total payouts around the 1998 introduction of repurchases in Germany, and additionally decompose the response into permanent and transitory earnings components. Their results reject the hypothesis that dividends and repurchases are perfect substitutes and find that repurchases have not taken over the role of special dividends; instead they support the flexibility hypothesis, under which regular dividends disburse permanent earnings while more flexible channels — special dividends and repurchases — disburse transitory earnings. The theoretical counterpart is lambrecht-2012-a-lintner-model-of-payout-and-managerial-rents, whose model delivers total payout following the Lintner target-adjustment form and adjusting gradually to permanent income while smoothing out transitory shocks, providing the permanent/transitory logic that the empirical decomposition tests. The empirical signature that separates the two views is whether a transitory earnings shock passes into regular dividends (perfect-substitution/single-stream view) or is routed to repurchases and specials while the regular dividend holds (flexibility view). Only two papers in this corpus estimate the total-payout extension directly, so this variant rests on a thinner base than the firm-type validation above. Current assessment (2026-07): In the repurchase era the dividend-only speed of adjustment measures the stickiness of one channel, not the smoothness of total distributions, and the evidence that dividends and repurchases are not perfect substitutes (andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts) means a dividend-only measure and a total-payout measure can diverge. Because the theory that motivates the whole apparatus concerns total payout (lambrecht-2012-a-lintner-model-of-payout-and-managerial-rents), the total-payout speed of adjustment is arguably the more theory-consistent object, but the dividend-only measure remains the one most comparable to the historical literature. No consensus has settled which is the "right" measure. Variants: structural and model-based measures A second family of variants abandons the single reduced-form coefficient in favor of structural or dynamic-model estimation that decomposes observed smoothness into its behavioral sources. wu-2018-what-s-behind-smooth-dividends-evidence-from-structural estimates a dynamic agency model in which dividends signal earnings persistence, and uses the fitted parameters to partition measured smoothness into a shareholder-preference component and a managerial-career-concern component — an exercise a reduced-form speed of adjustment cannot perform, since that single number pools all sources. A related model-based approach treats firm value as depending on payout smoothness within a dynamic partial-equilibrium framework, yielding smoothness as an equilibrium object rather than a regression residual (karpavicius-2014-dividends-relevance-rigidity-and-signaling). Alternative scalar metrics that sidestep the target-adjustment regression entirely include volatility ratios of dividends to earnings and, for asset-pricing purposes, smoothing-robust series such as net payout and earnings (chen-2012-dividend-smoothing-and-predictability). The empirical signature these variants add is a decomposition: rather than reporting how sticky dividends are, they report how much of the stickiness is attributable to a named economic force, which is what lets the smoothing literature move from measuring the phenomenon to adjudicating its causes. Known biases and comparability Estimated smoothing is not a clean measurement, and several biases limit cross-study comparison. First, repurchases contaminate dividend-only measures: because dividends and repurchases are not perfect substitutes, a dividend-only speed of adjustment can overstate the smoothness of total distributions (andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts). Second, smoothing induces a spurious relation between dividends and future performance — karpavicius-2014-dividends-relevance-rigidity-and-signaling show that the empirically observed positive dividend–future-performance link is a statistical artifact of smoothing, so signaling tests built on that correlation may be misspecified. Third, institutional timing inflates measured persistence: as nearly 60% of dividend increases come in fixed four-quarter cycles, dividend policy becomes mechanically more persistent, raising apparent smoothing for reasons unrelated to any deliberate target-adjustment choice (andres-2017-do-what-you-did-four-quarters-ago-trends). Fourth, smoothing biases asset-pricing inference by burying dividend-growth predictability, so the postwar failure to predict dividend growth reflects heavy smoothing rather than absent cash-flow news, and smoothing-robust measures recover a leading role for cash-flow news (chen-2012-dividend-smoothing-and-predictability); the cross-country evidence confirms that predictability is weaker precisely where dividends are smoothed more (rangvid-2014-dividend-predictability-around-the-world). Finally, cross-country and cross-firm comparability is limited because firm characteristics, tax regimes, and institutions that shape the estimated parameter differ systematically across samples (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing; chemmanur-2010-is-dividend-smoothing-universal-new-insights-from-a). Cross-paper pattern: Measured smoothing contaminates the very inferences it is used to draw. It manufactures a dividend–future-performance correlation that corrupts signaling tests (karpavicius-2014-dividends-relevance-rigidity-and-signaling) and it suppresses dividend-growth predictability in ways that corrupt cash-flow-versus-discount-rate inferences (chen-2012-dividend-smoothing-and-predictability; rangvid-2014-dividend-predictability-around-the-world). Any test that conditions on dividends must therefore treat the smoothing parameter as endogenous rather than as a clean regressor. Open questions Three measurement questions remain unresolved. The first is whether the dividend-only or the total-payout speed of adjustment is the correct object in the repurchase era, given that the two diverge once dividends and repurchases are imperfect substitutes (andres-2015-the-lintner-model-revisited-dividends-versus-total-payouts; lambrecht-2012-a-lintner-model-of-payout-and-managerial-rents). The second is how to separate deliberate smoothing from mechanical persistence, since fixed four-quarter announcement cycles inflate the estimated parameter without reflecting any target-adjustment decision (andres-2017-do-what-you-did-four-quarters-ago-trends) and structural decomposition is needed to isolate the behavioral component (wu-2018-what-s-behind-smooth-dividends-evidence-from-structural). The third is harmonizing measures across countries and datasets so that a speed of adjustment estimated in one institutional setting is comparable to another, given the firm-level and country-level heterogeneity that drives the parameter (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). These measurement choices feed directly into the substantive debates surveyed on dividend-smoothing. Standard operationalization of the propensity to pay
Composition vs. behavior: decomposing the trend
pages.excerpt: The payout literature rests on two workhorse dependent variables that answer different questions and must not be conflated. The payout ratio is an intensive-margin measure — how much a firm distributes, scaled by earnings, assets, or net income — while the propensity to pay is…
pages.text: Payout Ratio and Propensity to Pay The payout literature rests on two workhorse dependent variables that answer different questions and must not be conflated. The payout ratio is an intensive-margin measure — how much a firm distributes, scaled by earnings, assets, or net income — while the propensity to pay is an extensive-margin measure — whether a firm pays at all, most usefully the conditional propensity estimated after controlling for firm characteristics. The distinction is not pedantic: many apparent contradictions in the collection dissolve once the measure is pinned down, because dividends "disappear" on the extensive margin (fewer payers) even as aggregate dollars concentrate and rise, and net cash returned to shareholders does not decline at all. This page documents what each measure captures, the standard conditional-logit operationalization, the covariates that scale it, the composition-versus-behavior decomposition that reads the disappearing-dividends trend, the pivotal switch from a dividends-only to a total-payout denominator, cross-sample comparability, and the biases that trap the unwary. Its job is to define the operationalizations and flag the pitfalls, not to adjudicate the substantive debates these measures feed. What is being measured: intensive vs. extensive margin The two margins are logically independent. The intensive margin asks, conditional on paying, how large the distribution is relative to a base — the classic dividend payout ratio, or a broader total-payout ratio that adds repurchases to the numerator. The extensive margin asks a binary question — does the firm pay — and its aggregate counterpart is the proportion of firms that pay, which fell from 66.5% in 1978 to 20.8% in 1999 (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). A second, orthogonal choice concerns what is counted: dividends only, or total payout including repurchases, or net payout after equity issuance — formally $\text{net payout} = \text{dividends} + \text{repurchases} - \text{equity issuance}$. Because repurchases became the dominant payout form and dividend-only firms became largely extinct, a dividends-only measure increasingly mismeasures the underlying distribution behavior (skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). The net-cash measure — dividends plus repurchases minus issuance — behaves altogether differently from the dividend count, which is the single most consequential measurement fact in the disappearing-dividends debate (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined). Standard operationalization of the propensity to pay The canonical extensive-margin tool is the Fama–French conditional-logit approach: regress the pay/not-pay indicator on firm characteristics (size, profitability, growth, and the earned/contributed capital mix), then read the unexplained shift over time — the change in fitted probability holding characteristics fixed — as the change in propensity or proclivity net of composition. Schematically, the expected payer fraction is $\widehat{p}t = \frac{1}{N_t}\sum_i \Lambda(\hat{\beta}\,x{it})$ using base-period coefficients $\hat{\beta}$; the gap between the actual fraction and $\widehat{p}t$ isolates the behavioral component, while the movement of $\widehat{p}t$ itself captures the compositional component. The empirical signature that motivates the method is that the propensity falls even after characteristics are held constant, so the decline is not merely a story of the firm population changing (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). The same conditional framework travels internationally, where the propensity to pay is higher among larger, more profitable firms and those whose retained earnings form a large fraction of equity, across the US, Canada, UK, Germany, France, and Japan (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). Re-examination of the US series shows the method is sensitive to how the sample composition is treated: attributing the decline instead to the changing composition of firms over time, and surfacing an IPO-cohort effect whereby the decade a firm went public shapes its initial payout policy while a within-cohort lifecycle effect persists (banyi-2014-declining-propensity-to-pay-a-re-examination-of). Determinants that scale the measures The covariates in the conditional model are not nuisance controls; they define the benchmark of a "reasonable payer" against which propensity is judged. The dominant covariate is the earned/contributed capital mix — the fraction of equity that is retained earnings rather than contributed capital — which has a quantitatively greater impact on the decision to pay than profitability or growth opportunities (deangelo-2006-dividend-policy-and-the-earned-contributed-capital-mix). This is the empirical backbone of the lifecycle reading of payout: firms rich in earned equity are the reasonable candidates to pay, and it is exactly those firms whose propensity fell most, at roughly twice the overall Fama–French reduction (deangelo-2006-dividend-policy-and-the-earned-contributed-capital-mix). Profitability, size, and growth remain the standard supplementary covariates and carry the expected signs internationally, with larger and more profitable firms more likely to pay (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on; fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). Because these determinants both explain incidence and calibrate the intensive ratio, mis-specifying them contaminates both margins at once, which is why the earned/contributed mix has become a near-mandatory control. Composition vs. behavior: decomposing the trend The core inferential task is separating a changing firm population (composition) from a changing willingness to pay conditional on type (behavior/proclivity). The founding decomposition splits the 1978–1999 decline into a compositional tilt toward small, unprofitable, high-growth new listings and a genuine behavioral drop that holds regardless of characteristics, judging the latter at least as important (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). Extending through the reappearance, a later decomposition finds characteristics and proclivity each drive about half of the 1970s–2000 disappearance, while 82% of the 2000–2018 reappearance is driven by higher proclivity among stable, profitable firms and the residual 18% by reduced earnings volatility (michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). A structurally important finding for the decomposition is that newly listed and delisted firms — not initiations and omissions by continuing firms — drive the trends, which means the measure is as much about the entry and exit of firm-years as about behavior within a fixed panel (michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). The composition reading is reinforced by evidence tying the decline to the changing mix of firms and to IPO cohorts rather than to declining proclivity within firms, with the additional wrinkle that the propensity to pay was greater than expected following the 2003 dividend tax cut (banyi-2014-declining-propensity-to-pay-a-re-examination-of). The decomposition machinery therefore carries a genuine identification burden: the same aggregate series admits both a behavioral and a compositional reading depending on how firm entry and exit, IPO vintage, and tax-regime breaks are handled, and the two decompositions in the collection reach materially different weightings on proclivity versus composition even over overlapping windows (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity; banyi-2014-declining-propensity-to-pay-a-re-examination-of). This is why the conditional propensity, not the raw payer fraction, is the object the field actually models. Cross-paper pattern: Whether the disappearance is read as behavior or composition depends heavily on sample construction and horizon — Fama–French and Michaely–Moin assign a large role to falling proclivity, while the re-examination attributes it to the changing composition of firms and IPO-cohort effects (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity; michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends; banyi-2014-declining-propensity-to-pay-a-re-examination-of). Dividends-only vs. total net payout Switching the numerator from dividends to net cash distributed to equity holders overturns the headline conclusion. When the measure is net payout — dividends plus repurchases net of equity issuance — there is no evidence that the conditional propensity to distribute has declined over three decades; net payout yields have actually increased conditional on characteristics (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined). This is consistent with the substitution of repurchases for dividends and with total payout remaining anchored to earnings even as the dividend-only series fell (skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). It also reconciles with the worldwide picture, where a dividends-only lens still shows a real decline in both the average payout ratio and the proportion of payers even after controlling for characteristics — most pronounced among smaller, less profitable, higher-growth firms and in civil-law countries — precisely because that lens excludes the repurchase channel that absorbs the difference elsewhere (fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). A recurrent aggregate fact spanning these studies is that dividend dollars are highly concentrated in a small group of the largest, most profitable firms, so firm-count measures and dollar-weighted measures can move in opposite directions (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on; fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). Cross-country and cross-sample comparability Comparability across studies hinges on aligning both the numerator definition and the legal-institutional setting. A worldwide sample of more than 17,000 firms across 33 countries documents a genuine decline in the propensity to pay after controlling for characteristics, but with the decline in mean payout ratios and payer proportions far more pronounced in civil-law countries than common-law ones — a reminder that a pooled payout ratio blends behavior with legal environment (fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). The six-country evidence sharpens the point: the same conditional-propensity apparatus yields the familiar size/profitability/earned-equity gradient everywhere, but the apparent reductions in propensity are driven largely by newly listed firms failing to initiate when expected, and dividend abandonment by existing payers is economically unimportant except in Japan (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). The practical upshot is that comparing a payout ratio across countries or samples without harmonizing the payout definition, the treatment of new listings, and the legal regime risks attributing to behavior what is really a difference in measurement or institutions. Known biases and pitfalls Several recurring traps distort inference. The first is treating incidence as intensity — reporting a falling fraction of payers as though total distributions fell, when aggregate and net-payout dollars rose (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined; fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). The second is an aggregation trap: because dividends concentrate in a few large firms, an equal-weighted firm-count measure and a dollar-weighted measure can diverge, so the choice of weighting is itself a modeling decision (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). The third is survivorship and turnover, since listing and delisting of firm-years — not within-firm decisions — drive much of the observed trend, so a measure computed on a survivor panel misstates the population dynamics (michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). The fourth is the choice of scaling denominator (earnings, assets, or price) and of numerator (dividends, total payout, or net payout), which can flip the sign of the trend (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined; skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). A fifth trap is treating the conditional propensity as invariant to sample construction, when in fact the estimated proclivity depends on how new listings and IPO cohorts are handled: a decline that looks behavioral in one specification reads as compositional once the entry decade is modeled (banyi-2014-declining-propensity-to-pay-a-re-examination-of; michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). A sixth, cross-country, trap is pooling civil- and common-law firms into a single ratio, since the payout-ratio decline is far sharper under civil law and pooling attributes to behavior what is partly institutional (fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). Current assessment (2026-07): For the incidence question the conditional propensity to pay dividends (Fama–French logit) remains canonical, but for the substance question — has the firm reduced what it returns to shareholders — the field now treats the conditional net-payout measure as the appropriate variable, since it is the one that does not spuriously register the dividend-to-repurchase form shift as a decline. pages.excerpt: The disclosure-and-information-environment channel is the causal pathway through which the quality, transparency, and asymmetry of firm-level information shape payout policy, and, reciprocally, through which payout itself operates as information. Two logically opposed…
pages.text: Disclosure and the Information Environment Channel The disclosure-and-information-environment channel is the causal pathway through which the quality, transparency, and asymmetry of firm-level information shape payout policy, and, reciprocally, through which payout itself operates as information. Two logically opposed micro-foundations sit under this heading: an outcome channel, in which transparent reporting lets shareholders measure and therefore demand distribution of excess cash, and a substitute channel, in which opacity raises managers' incentive to pay out in order to build a reputation for fair treatment. Overlaid on both is the classical signaling role, in which dividends convey private information about permanent earnings precisely when other information channels are weak. Because the same dividend can carry opposite meanings across information regimes, this channel reconciles the long-standing weakness of dividend-signaling tests in transparent samples with strong signaling evidence in opaque ones. This article treats the mechanism itself: how information asymmetry moderates the link between cash flows and payout, the opposed transparency micro-foundations, reporting quality as a governance device, dividends as an earnings-quality signal, the settings where the signal is strongest, the shocks that identify the channel, and the scope conditions under which it weakens. The causal channel: information as moderator At the core of the channel is a single structural claim: information asymmetry sits between a firm's underlying cash flows and its observed payout, so that the interpretation and the level of a dividend both depend on how much shareholders can independently observe. When outside investors cannot cheaply verify free cash flow, a dividend does double duty, transferring cash and revealing information that would otherwise stay private. The empirical signature is a moderation pattern: the informativeness of a dividend change should rise as the surrounding information environment deteriorates and fall as it improves. Cross-listed firms with fewer alternative information channels use dividend increases as a more credible signal (aggarwal-2012-information-environment-dividend-changes-and-signaling-evidence-from); in opaque markets, stock liquidity that supplies information raises insiders' incentive to distribute (jiang-2017-stock-liquidity-and-dividend-payouts); and as sophisticated institutional holders erode the informational scarcity that once made dividends surprising, announcement reactions shrink (amihud-2006-the-declining-information-content-of-dividend-announcements-and). The same logic drives payout levels: disclosure transparency changes how well shareholders can measure the excess cash they might demand (brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). Cross-paper pattern: Across the cross-listing, liquidity, and institutional-holdings literatures, the informativeness of a dividend change moves inversely with the richness of the information environment — stronger where alternative channels are scarce (aggarwal-2012-information-environment-dividend-changes-and-signaling-evidence-from; jiang-2017-stock-liquidity-and-dividend-payouts) and weaker where sophisticated investors already price the information (amihud-2006-the-declining-information-content-of-dividend-announcements-and). Outcome versus substitute micro-foundations The channel's defining tension is that transparency can push payout in either direction, and both directions are empirically supported. The outcome hypothesis holds that transparent disclosure environments raise dividends because shareholders can more accurately measure, and therefore demand distribution of, excess cash flows. The substitute hypothesis holds that opaque environments raise payout because managers have stronger incentives to establish a reputation for fair treatment when outsiders cannot verify their behavior directly. Testing the agency-cost version of the dividend lifecycle theory against cross-country disclosure variation, brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality confirms both hypotheses, concluding that the disclosure environment shapes payout through its effect on agency costs and yielding what the study terms an "agency cost-inclusive lifecycle theory of dividends." The two micro-foundations are not contradictory once agency costs are the mediating variable: transparency lowers the cost of demanding cash (outcome), while opacity raises the private return to a fair-treatment reputation (substitute). This duality generates a sharp testable prediction — the sign of the disclosure–payout relation depends on which mechanism dominates in a given regime, and both the reputation-building logic in weak-protection settings (he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries) and the liquidity-as-information logic in opaque markets (jiang-2017-stock-liquidity-and-dividend-payouts) reflect the substitute side, while reporting-quality effects in developed markets (koo-2017-the-effect-of-financial-reporting-quality-on-corporate) reflect the outcome side. Reporting quality as a governance mechanism Where the outcome channel operates, higher-quality financial reporting functions as a governance device that disciplines free cash flow and thereby raises dividends. Higher reporting quality is associated with higher dividends, and this positive association is more pronounced among firms with more severe free-cash-flow problems and among firms with higher ownership by monitoring-type institutional investors (koo-2017-the-effect-of-financial-reporting-quality-on-corporate). The same study pins down direction: reporting quality largely mitigates the underpayment of dividends, and both a Granger-causality test and a difference-in-differences analysis around a quasi-exogenous reporting event point from reporting quality to dividends rather than the reverse, consistent with the Jensen free-cash-flow and La Porta outcome-model views that dividends result from enhanced monitoring. Reporting quality is not the only accounting attribute that substitutes for the disciplining role of payout: accounting conservatism reduces the need for dividends because it independently curbs managers' incentives to fund value-destroying projects, and this conservatism effect strengthens with the potential agency conflict between managers and shareholders (louis-2015-agency-conflicts-dividend-payout-and-the-direct-benefits). The reputation channel appears cross-nationally as well: dividend payers manage earnings less than non-payers, an association that is stronger in countries with weak investor protection and high opacity, consistent with firms using low-manipulation dividend policies to establish credible reputations and ease access to external funds (he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries). Together these results place reporting quality, conservatism, and payout as partially interchangeable governance instruments whose relative weight depends on the information regime. Dividends as a signal of earnings quality The reciprocal direction of the channel is that payout itself informs on earnings quality. The reported earnings of dividend-paying firms are more persistent than those of other firms, a relation that is remarkably stable over roughly three decades; payers are also less likely to report losses, and the losses they do report tend to be transitory, driven by special items (skinner-2011-what-do-dividends-tell-us-about-earnings-quality). This informativeness is weaker for stock repurchases, consistent with repurchases representing less of a commitment than dividends. The signal appears to substitute for accounting information rather than merely complement it: dividend-paying firms have earnings response coefficients 11–15% lower than non-payers, with more substitution when the dividend gives a stronger signal of permanent earnings — when the firm is less likely to cut, when it funds the dividend out of earnings rather than reserves, or when the dividend is larger (ham-2023-attention-to-dividends-inattention-to-earnings). The same study shows payers attract less attention at earnings announcements (lower absolute returns, less volume, fewer analyst forecasts), which in turn translates into less earnings management and fewer earnings-related disclosures. Auditors price this information: dividend-paying clients receive audit-fee discounts of roughly 6–11%, and dividends interact with earnings persistence and manipulation risk in setting fees (lawson-2016-the-earnings-quality-information-content-of-dividend-policies). Dividend changes carry information about highly persistent changes in future economic income, though the timing of that information content is difficult to reconcile with traditional signaling models (ham-2020-do-dividends-convey-information-about-future-earnings). Cross-paper pattern: Across the accounting literature, dividend payers exhibit higher-quality earnings — more persistent, less loss-prone, less managed (skinner-2011-what-do-dividends-tell-us-about-earnings-quality; he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries; ham-2023-attention-to-dividends-inattention-to-earnings; lawson-2016-the-earnings-quality-information-content-of-dividend-policies) — and the association is systematically weaker for repurchases, which commit less. When the signal is strongest: poor information environments The moderation logic predicts that dividends carry the most information exactly where other channels are weakest, and the cross-listing evidence isolates this. Theory long held that dividends should be a credible performance signal, yet signaling tests among U.S. firms were weak, plausibly because cross-sectional variation in information asymmetry across U.S. firms is too small to give tests adequate power (aggarwal-2012-information-environment-dividend-changes-and-signaling-evidence-from). Examining foreign firms that cross-list in the U.S. as American Depository Receipts, the same study finds that ADR firms with poorer information environments have stronger incentives to use dividend increases as a credible signaling device; such firms experience an increase in one-year-ahead earnings and a decline in systematic risk following a dividend increase, and they have fewer other information channels than comparable U.S. firms. Opacity and the controlling–minority-shareholder conflict act as amplifiers elsewhere: the positive stock-liquidity–payout relation is more pronounced when the information environment is opaque and when conflict between controlling and minority shareholders is severe (jiang-2017-stock-liquidity-and-dividend-payouts), and the reputation-building, low-manipulation payout pattern is concentrated in weak-protection, high-opacity countries (he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries). This is the substitute side of brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality made observable: where verification is hard, payout does more informational work. Shocks to information asymmetry and monitoring Because information asymmetry is endogenous to payout, the sharpest evidence for the channel comes from shocks that move monitoring or asymmetry from outside the firm. The initiation of credit-default-swap trading is one such shock: CDS initiation is associated with increasing dividends, consistent with firms distributing excess free cash flow to offset the manager–equityholder agency conflict that intensifies when banks, now hedged, monitor less (landsman-2023-cds-trading-initiation-information-asymmetry-and-dividend-payout). The dividend increases concentrate among borrowers with higher pre-initiation agency cost, those whose lead-arranger banks have weaker syndication-market reputations, and those whose loans carry less restrictive covenants afterward — a pattern tying payout tightly to the monitoring loss. A second shock runs the other way: the secular rise of sophisticated, informed institutional holders reduces the information content of dividends, lowering cumulative abnormal returns at dividend-change announcements since the mid-1970s, with the reaction decreasing in institutional holdings; such investors trade on superior information ahead of increases, and high-institutional-holdings firms are less likely to raise dividends at all (amihud-2006-the-declining-information-content-of-dividend-announcements-and). Regulation can substitute for the informational role of markets: market reactions to rules mandating payout are more favorable for low-liquidity firms, implying that legal provisions and stock liquidity are substitutes in supplying the discipline and information behind dividends (jiang-2017-stock-liquidity-and-dividend-payouts). Reporting-event shocks complete the picture, with difference-in-differences evidence that improved reporting quality raises subsequent dividends (koo-2017-the-effect-of-financial-reporting-quality-on-corporate). Scope conditions and failure modes The channel weakens or reverses under identifiable conditions. When the investor base is sophisticated and informed, dividends lose their scarcity value as a signal, so announcement informativeness falls and firms substitute away from dividends (amihud-2006-the-declining-information-content-of-dividend-announcements-and). Payout form matters: repurchases carry a weaker earnings-quality signal than dividends because they commit less, muting the informational relation (skinner-2011-what-do-dividends-tell-us-about-earnings-quality; lawson-2016-the-earnings-quality-information-content-of-dividend-policies). Attention is a further boundary: because payers draw less scrutiny to their earnings announcements, the very act of paying can displace the demand for earnings information that would otherwise discipline reporting, so the signal is efficient for some firms but costly, and its value depends on the strength of the permanent-earnings signal it conveys (ham-2023-attention-to-dividends-inattention-to-earnings). Where substitute accounting mechanisms are strong, conservatism can absorb the disciplining role and reduce the payout the channel would otherwise produce (louis-2015-agency-conflicts-dividend-payout-and-the-direct-benefits). Finally, the timing of the information content in dividend changes fits imperfectly with traditional signaling models, a reminder that the channel is better described as information moderation than as a clean costly-signal equilibrium (ham-2020-do-dividends-convey-information-about-future-earnings). Current assessment (2026-07): The evidence that information asymmetry moderates both the level and the informativeness of payout is strong and multi-sourced, spanning cross-country disclosure variation, cross-listing, liquidity, reporting-quality, and monitoring shocks. The declining announcement reaction in sophisticated markets is the clearest failure mode: as alternative information channels thicken, the dividend's marginal informational role fades. The open question is how to reconcile the observed timing of dividends' information content with formal signaling models. pages.title: Disgorging Free Cash Flow
headings: Repurchases versus dividends as disgorgement vehicles
The disgorgement–retention margin in dynamic models
pages.excerpt: Disgorging free cash flow is the causal channel by which a cash distribution — a dividend increase, a special dividend, or a share repurchase — physically removes surplus cash from managerial control and thereby shrinks the resources available for overinvestment or waste. Where…
pages.text: Disgorging Free Cash Flow Disgorging free cash flow is the causal channel by which a cash distribution — a dividend increase, a special dividend, or a share repurchase — physically removes surplus cash from managerial control and thereby shrinks the resources available for overinvestment or waste. Where agency-costs-of-free-cash-flow names the problem, disgorgement names the direct remedy: the distribution is valuable not (or not only) for what it signals but because the cash is gone. The mechanism is analytically distinct from the recurring-commitment channel that forces firms back to capital markets (dividends-as-bonding-device) and from the information channel of dividend signalling (dividend-signaling); its own empirical signature is that payout announcements are revalued most where the disgorged cash would otherwise have been most likely to be squandered — high surplus funds combined with poor investment opportunities and weak internal controls. This page isolates the cash-removal channel: how it works, the announcement-return fingerprints that identify it, why repurchases and dividends differ as disgorgement vehicles, what forces the disgorgement in the first place, its treatment at the retention margin in dynamic models, its aggregate and lifecycle expression, and the conditions under which disgorgement fails or is undone. The causal channel The mechanism is mechanical in the most literal sense: cash paid out is cash no longer available to fund discretionary spending. A one-time disgorgement is the cleanest form of the channel, because it removes a stock of surplus without embedding a recurring promise. Special dividends and self-tender offers target funds that are largely nonrecurring — cash accumulated above industry norms — whereas regular dividend increases target recurring cash and tend to be smaller (lie-2000-excess-funds-and-agency-problems-an-empirical-study). This distinction matters for the channel's logic: it is the removal of a discrete accumulated stock of surplus, not the trimming of the ongoing flow, that most directly shrinks the resources available for empire-building. Share repurchases work the same way, alleviating the agency costs of surplus cash by "restricting management's scope to waste corporate resources," and the interesting behavioural question is not whether removal helps but why self-interested managers ever agree to it (oswald-2008-share-reacquisitions-surplus-cash-and-agency-problems). The disciplinary content of the channel is visible even in individual cases: at Times Mirror, stockholder value rose substantially once a new CEO terminated low-return investments and distributed free cash flow, the surplus having previously funded a reinvestment plan the market disliked (deangelo-2000-controlling-stockholders-and-the-disciplinary-role-of-corporate). That episode also shows the channel is instrument-agnostic — value is created by the physical removal and reallocation of cash away from low-return uses, whatever the payout label. The channel should be kept distinct from precommitment: disgorgement operates on the level of cash removed today, not on the discipline a standing commitment imposes tomorrow — the recurring-commitment logic belongs to dividends-as-bonding-device. Empirical signatures in announcement returns The mechanism yields a sharp, testable prediction: the value gain from a distribution should rise with the product of surplus cash and poor investment opportunities. The evidence bears this out through several independent designs. The stock-price reaction to large disbursements is positively related to the level of excess funds for self-tender offers and large special dividends (lie-2000-excess-funds-and-agency-problems-an-empirical-study). Dividend-initiation announcement returns are significantly more positive for firms with low Tobin's Q and high cash flow — the classic overinvestor — which is read as the market pricing a reduction in overinvestment agency costs (officer-2011-overinvestment-corporate-governance-and-dividend-initiations). Repurchase announcements draw a more positive reaction among firms more likely to overinvest, consistent with the free-cash-flow hypothesis (grullon-2004-the-information-content-of-share-repurchase-programs). And low-growth firms disgorge cash irrespective of controller identity, with the payout concentrated where reinvestment opportunities are weakest (gugler-2003-corporate-governance-dividend-payout-policy-and-the-interrelation). Crucially, the same repurchase study finds that announcements are not followed by improved operating performance, which weakens the competing operating-signal reading and strengthens the cash-removal interpretation; the documented gains instead take the form of a reduction in systematic risk and cost of capital, to which investors under-react (grullon-2004-the-information-content-of-share-repurchase-programs). The design logic that unifies these tests is a difference-in-differences in cross-section: hold the payout event fixed and let the overinvestment potential vary, and the revaluation tracks the potential — the signature the pure cash-removal channel predicts and the alternatives do not. Cross-paper pattern: Across the disgorgement literature, the announcement revaluation scales with surplus cash × poor opportunities rather than with either alone, and it appears for large, discretionary disbursements but not for small recurring ones (lie-2000-excess-funds-and-agency-problems-an-empirical-study; officer-2011-overinvestment-corporate-governance-and-dividend-initiations; grullon-2004-the-information-content-of-share-repurchase-programs). Repurchases versus dividends as disgorgement vehicles For one-off surplus, managers frequently prefer repurchases to dividend increases, because a repurchase removes cash without embedding a future payout commitment that would constrain the firm in later periods. Firms with weaker governance, when they do distribute, choose repurchases over dividend increases precisely to avoid future payout commitments (harford-2008-corporate-governance-and-firm-cash-holdings-in-the). The choice tracks the nature of the surplus: repurchases are used disproportionately by firms with higher temporary, non-operating cash flows and more volatile cash flows and distributions, and are pro-cyclical and timed to follow poor stock-market performance, while dividends are paid out of higher permanent operating cash flow — so the flexibility of the buyback is exactly what makes it the vehicle for removing a nonrecurring stock of surplus (jagannathan-2000-financial-flexibility-and-the-choice-between-dividends-and). This makes the repurchase the natural vehicle for the pure cash-removal channel, uncontaminated by the recurring-commitment logic. But it also raises the puzzle of why self-interested managers agree to disgorge at all: the decision to distribute excess cash through a repurchase is intermediated by governance, and repurchases substitute for cash-retention decisions that would otherwise be costly to shareholders, with better managerial incentive alignment and closer monitoring by external shareholders being important factors that stimulate such payouts (oswald-2008-share-reacquisitions-surplus-cash-and-agency-problems). Compensation design pushes the same way: management stock ownership raises payout most at the firms with the greatest agency problems — low insider ownership combined with few investment opportunities or high free cash flow — while stock options relate positively to repurchases and negatively to dividends, so the growth of option pay plausibly channels disgorgement into the commitment-free buyback form (fenn-2001-corporate-payout-policy-and-managerial-stock-incentives). The revaluation gains reinforce the choice, since the overinvestor repurchase premium documents that the market rewards exactly the firms where the cash-removal benefit is largest (grullon-2004-the-information-content-of-share-repurchase-programs). Cross-paper pattern: Where the surplus is nonrecurring, the repurchase is the preferred disgorgement vehicle because it removes cash without a standing commitment — a preference sharpest at weakly governed firms (harford-2008-corporate-governance-and-firm-cash-holdings-in-the; oswald-2008-share-reacquisitions-surplus-cash-and-agency-problems). What forces the disgorgement The remedy is not automatic; self-interested managers rarely disgorge surplus on their own initiative, so the channel requires a trigger. Incentive alignment and monitoring supply one: closer external-shareholder monitoring and better-aligned managerial incentives raise the probability that surplus cash is returned rather than retained (oswald-2008-share-reacquisitions-surplus-cash-and-agency-problems). Managerial equity ownership is a concrete form of that alignment — payouts are highest precisely at the firms with the greatest agency potential, those combining low management stock ownership with poor investment opportunities or high free cash flow, so raising insider ownership pulls surplus out of exactly the overinvestment-prone firms where disgorgement matters most (fenn-2001-corporate-payout-policy-and-managerial-stock-incentives). Block-stockholder pressure supplies another, though its bite is weaker and slower than theory suggests — at Times Mirror, pressure to pay dividends and monitoring by large block stockholders ultimately worked, but the path was "slow and circuitous," so the disciplinary forces proved weaker than typically implied (deangelo-2000-controlling-stockholders-and-the-disciplinary-role-of-corporate). Exogenous shocks can force disgorgement where internal governance will not: the Undistributed Profits Tax of 1936–37 taxed retained earnings and produced a positive equity revaluation concentrated at lower-payout firms, yet managers most exposed to agency costs still resisted, growing dividends less than others despite the tax incentive (christie-1994-free-cash-flow-shareholder-value-and-the-undistributed). Finally, poor investment opportunities themselves act as a trigger, since low-growth firms optimally disgorge regardless of who controls them (gugler-2003-corporate-governance-dividend-payout-policy-and-the-interrelation). The disgorgement–retention margin in dynamic models The channel does not imply that all surplus should be forced out immediately; external-financing costs make retained cash valuable, so there is an optimal disgorgement rate. A dynamic model of a firm facing agency costs of free cash flow and external-financing costs solves explicitly for optimal balance-sheet dynamics, showing that financial frictions jointly shape issuance and dividend policies and the value of cash holdings (dcamps-2011-free-cash-flow-issuance-costs-and-stock-prices). Because the marginal value of internal cash exceeds one when the stock price is low and rises with volatility, the optimal policy retains a buffer rather than disgorging to zero — disgorging the full surplus can be costly when re-raising external funds is expensive (dcamps-2011-free-cash-flow-issuance-costs-and-stock-prices). This sets the retention margin: cash should be disgorged up to the point where the agency benefit of removal equals the marginal value of precautionary cash net of issuance costs. The framing reconciles the channel with the observation that cash-rich firms do not disgorge everything: some retention is optimal precautionary policy rather than agency-driven hoarding, and only surplus above the precautionary buffer is the proper object of the free-cash-flow remedy. Empirically, the margin shifts with opportunities, so low-growth firms sit closer to full disgorgement while high-growth firms optimally retain (gugler-2003-corporate-governance-dividend-payout-policy-and-the-interrelation). The same frictions explain why the excess-funds relation appears for large, nonrecurring disbursements but not for small recurring ones: only a disbursement large relative to the buffer moves cash across the agency-relevant margin (lie-2000-excess-funds-and-agency-problems-an-empirical-study). Aggregate and lifecycle patterns At the aggregate level, disgorgement is the payout supply of distribution-phase firms. Mature, cash-generative firms with limited reinvestment need dominate public equity markets as a percent of value and of earnings, and they account for the bulk of aggregate payouts; the composition of that supply, the profitability of payers, and aggregate payout rates have all shifted since the 1980s (deangelo-2025-agency-cost-of-free-cash-flow-capital-allocation). This lifecycle mapping matters for the mechanism because it locates disgorgement where the free-cash-flow problem is quantitatively largest: the firms with the least reinvestment need and the most internally generated cash are precisely the large, profitable incumbents that carry most of the market's value, so the cash-removal channel is a first-order feature of aggregate payout rather than a corner case. The rise of repurchases as a payout form maps directly onto the cash-removal channel, since repurchases are the flexible, commitment-free way to return nonrecurring surplus (grullon-2004-the-information-content-of-share-repurchase-programs; harford-2008-corporate-governance-and-firm-cash-holdings-in-the). That rise is partly substitution rather than net addition: firms finance repurchases with funds that would otherwise have gone to higher dividends, repurchases have become the preferred form of initiating a cash payout, and even large established firms increasingly disburse through buybacks — so the aggregate shift toward repurchases is the disgorgement channel selecting the instrument that removes surplus without a standing commitment (grullon-2002-dividends-share-repurchases-and-the-substitution-hypothesis). The recent politicisation of share repurchases underscores that large-scale disgorgement is publicly contested, even as the finance evidence reads it as value-enhancing at overinvesting firms (deangelo-2025-agency-cost-of-free-cash-flow-capital-allocation). Failure modes and boundary cases Disgorgement can fail to occur, be too small to matter, or be undone. Recurring dividend increases are frequently too small to remove meaningful surplus, which is why their announcement returns are unrelated to excess funds while large special dividends and self-tenders show the excess-funds relation (lie-2000-excess-funds-and-agency-problems-an-empirical-study). Entrenched managers resist disgorgement even under strong incentives, as the muted dividend response to the 1936 tax shows (christie-1994-free-cash-flow-shareholder-value-and-the-undistributed), and where block pressure does work it can be slow and incomplete (deangelo-2000-controlling-stockholders-and-the-disciplinary-role-of-corporate). The most important boundary case concerns what weakly governed firms do instead of disgorging: rather than hoarding surplus, U.S. firms with weak shareholder rights hold smaller cash reserves and spend excess cash quickly on acquisitions and capital expenditure, so the failure of disgorgement shows up as fast value-destroying spending rather than as a growing cash pile (harford-2008-corporate-governance-and-firm-cash-holdings-in-the). Current assessment (2026-07): The cash-removal channel is well identified for large, discretionary disbursements at overinvestors, but its failure mode is empirically the more consequential case: weakly governed firms tend not to hoard undisgorged surplus but to spend it fast on acquisitions and capex (harford-2008-corporate-governance-and-firm-cash-holdings-in-the), and the disciplinary triggers that would force disgorgement are slower and weaker than theory implies (deangelo-2000-controlling-stockholders-and-the-disciplinary-role-of-corporate).
