pages.title: Bank Payout and Prudential Regulation
headings: Dividend bans, capital, and credit supply
pages.excerpt: Payout policy at banks is a different object than at nonfinancial firms because leverage, deposit insurance, and prudential capital regulation change who bears the cost of a distribution. A bank dividend erodes regulatory capital and transfers value from creditors — and, through…
pages.text: Bank Payout and Prudential Regulation Payout policy at banks is a different object than at nonfinancial firms because leverage, deposit insurance, and prudential capital regulation change who bears the cost of a distribution. A bank dividend erodes regulatory capital and transfers value from creditors — and, through deposit insurance, from the insurance fund and ultimately the taxpayer — to shareholders, so a payout is partly a risk-shifting device rather than only a disgorgement of free cash flow or a signal of quality. This reframes the classical payout theories: the free-cash-flow and signaling accounts still operate, but they now sit alongside a motive unique to leveraged, insured institutions, and they coexist with a regulator empowered to override the payout choice directly. That regulatory override is what makes banks an unusually informative laboratory — it produces rare causal evidence on what payout is for and on who its costs fall on. The page treats four interlocking themes: why bank payout differs, payout as risk-shifting, whether capital regulation and supervision actually bind the payout choice, and bank dividends as signals to depositors and markets — before turning to the crisis-era restrictions, stress-test constraints, and outright dividend bans that made the subject acutely policy-relevant during 2007–09 and the 2020 COVID-19 shock. Why bank payout is different The defining feature of bank payout is that the shareholder–manager axis of nonfinancial payout is joined by additional claimants: creditors, the deposit-insurance fund, and the taxpayer. Because a distribution erodes equity capital, it directly affects the relative value of the competing claims on a bank, and when banks hold contingent claims on one another, one bank's capital policy affects the equity value and default risk of others (acharya-2017-bank-capital-and-dividend-externalities). Where these externalities are strong, bank capital becomes a public good, so the private equilibrium features excessive dividends and inefficient recapitalization relative to the sector-efficient policy that would maximize total banking-sector equity — a wedge with no counterpart in nonfinancial payout (acharya-2017-bank-capital-and-dividend-externalities). At the level of a single institution, paying out leaves riskier and less liquid assets behind to repay debtholders in the future, so a distribution mechanically transfers risk from equity to debt (srivastav-2014-ceo-inside-debt-holdings-and-risk-shifting-evidence; pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from). Even the standard nonfinancial determinants continue to apply: for 462 U.S. bank holding companies before and during the 2007–09 crisis, Fama–French characteristics — size, profitability, and growth opportunities — explain payout, and the agency-cost hypothesis explains it before and (more pronouncedly) during the crisis (abreu-2013-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-us-bank-holding-companies). Bank payout, then, is best read as the ordinary determinants plus a risk-shifting overlay plus an externality across interconnected institutions. Payout as risk-shifting The central mechanism distinctive to banks is risk-shifting: because a distribution benefits equity holders at the expense of debtholders and the insurance fund, the value investors attach to bank payout can reflect the ability to shift risk rather than the ability to reduce agency costs. The cleanest evidence comes from regulatory enforcement actions that restrict bank dividends and repurchases: abnormal stock returns around these actions are significantly worse for enforced banks that pay out than for those that do not, and — withstanding alternative explanations and parallel-trend concerns — this constitutes rare causal evidence of a value to distribution (pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from). The cross-section of abnormal returns points to risk-shifting, not agency-cost reduction, as the driver, and the ability to shift risk through payout is especially valuable among distressed banks around financial crises (pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from). Manager incentives that align with creditors dampen this motive: CEOs with higher inside debt (defined-benefit pensions and deferred compensation) relative to inside equity adopt more conservative payout — more likely to cut, and to cut by larger amounts, through both dividends and repurchases — and the result holds in the TARP subsample, where the risk-shift runs from the taxpayer to equity holders (srivastav-2014-ceo-inside-debt-holdings-and-risk-shifting-evidence). Regime evidence corroborates the motive at the sector level: over 1992–2008, the post-PCA period shows strong evidence of both risk-shifting and risk-taking, with risk-taking appearing just before the crisis (kanas-2013-bank-dividends-risk-and-regulatory-regimes). Cross-paper pattern: Across enforcement-action, inside-debt, and regulatory-regime designs, bank payout carries a risk-shifting motive distinct from the nonfinancial free-cash-flow/agency logic — distribution transfers value and risk from creditors, the insurance fund, and the taxpayer to shareholders, its value is highest for distressed banks near crises, and it is disciplined when managers' own claims are debt-like (pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from; srivastav-2014-ceo-inside-debt-holdings-and-risk-shifting-evidence; kanas-2013-bank-dividends-risk-and-regulatory-regimes). Capital regulation and supervisory constraints Given the risk-shifting motive, the natural question is whether prudential rules actually bind the payout choice — and the recurring finding before explicit restrictions is that they do not. Regulatory pressure was ineffective in limiting dividend payouts by undercapitalized banks before the 2007–09 crisis, even though those are precisely the banks whose payouts most threaten creditors and the insurance fund (abreu-2013-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-us-bank-holding-companies). The regime evidence reaches a parallel verdict on the prompt-corrective-action framework: the strong post-PCA risk-shifting and risk-taking over 1992–2008 indicate that PCA was ineffective at controlling risk-taking, with implications for Basel III (kanas-2013-bank-dividends-risk-and-regulatory-regimes). When capital ratios did rise after the crisis, the adjustment ran largely through retained earnings rather than through binding payout rules: for 101 large advanced- and emerging-economy banks, retained earnings account for the bulk of higher risk-weighted capital ratios, and lower dividend payouts — together with wider lending spreads at advanced-economy banks — are the channel through which banks built capital, while banks that emerged with higher capital and stronger profitability expanded lending more (cohen-2016-banks-and-capital-requirements-channels-of-adjustment). The picture is one of a payout margin that supervision struggles to constrain through ordinary pressure, yet that banks themselves throttle to rebuild capital when doing so serves their own recovery — a distinction that motivates the explicit restrictions treated below. Cross-paper pattern: Ordinary prudential pressure and prompt-corrective-action machinery are repeatedly found ineffective at binding bank payout absent explicit restrictions — undercapitalized banks kept paying pre-crisis and PCA did not control risk-taking — even though banks did curtail payout to rebuild capital through retained earnings when it served their own recovery (abreu-2013-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-us-bank-holding-companies; kanas-2013-bank-dividends-risk-and-regulatory-regimes; cohen-2016-banks-and-capital-requirements-channels-of-adjustment). Bank dividends as signals Alongside risk-shifting, bank dividends carry an information role, but the audience differs from the nonfinancial case: the informed party a bank most needs to reassure is its depositors and information-sensitive creditors, not only its shareholders. Exploiting an exogenous shock to the asset opaqueness of Brazilian banks during the 2008 turmoil, and using the cross-sectional heterogeneity of depositor types together with owner-managed banks — for which shareholder-targeted signaling is implausible — dividends are shown to signal asset quality and liquidity to information-sensitive depositors (institutional investors), with the costly signaling especially strong during crises when opaqueness and liquidity concerns peak (forti-2015-bank-dividends-and-signaling-to-information-sensitive-depositors). U.S. bank holding company data over 1986–2020 corroborate the information content: dividends lagged one quarter positively predict current-quarter financial health, and the relationship is more pronounced for banks with lower capital adequacy and during the 2007–09 crisis — precisely the banks and periods for which conveying health is most necessary — with the pattern extending to total payout and, more weakly, to private banks (tripathy-2021-dividends-and-financial-health-evidence-from-us-bank). The signaling hypothesis also explains payout specifically during the crisis in the BHC sample, alongside the agency and Fama–French channels (abreu-2013-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-us-bank-holding-companies). Signaling and risk-shifting are not mutually exclusive readings of the same distribution: a crisis-period dividend can simultaneously reassure depositors about health and shift residual risk onto creditors, which is why the depositor-signaling evidence itself favours limits on bank dividends during crises — the need to signal intensifies the pro-cyclical effect of bank capital on lending (forti-2015-bank-dividends-and-signaling-to-information-sensitive-depositors). Crisis-era restrictions and stress-test constraints When ordinary supervision does not bind payout, regulators turn to explicit restrictions, and the 2020 stress tests provide a clean reading of how markets price them. Banks subject to the 2020 stress tests and payout restrictions experienced both immediate and persistently lower excess stock returns, and in the cross-section the excess-return decline rose with bank size but was otherwise unexplained by pre-pandemic bank or payout characteristics — consistent with investors penalizing banks likely to face greater regulatory scrutiny rather than reacting to fundamentals (marsh-2023-supervisory-stringency-payout-restrictions-and-bank-equity-prices). Crucially, the penalty is smaller than that previously estimated for voluntary payout reductions that signal distress, so using supervisory discretion to take preventative action in a crisis is less costly than actions taken once banks are already distressed (marsh-2023-supervisory-stringency-payout-restrictions-and-bank-equity-prices). This is the empirical mirror image of the signaling channel: a mandated cut, imposed on all covered banks at once, does not carry the adverse-selection stigma that an individual bank's voluntary cut would, because it is not read as private bad news — a contrast that sharpens the case for pre-emptive supervisory restriction over waiting for distress-driven voluntary cuts (marsh-2023-supervisory-stringency-payout-restrictions-and-bank-equity-prices; forti-2015-bank-dividends-and-signaling-to-information-sensitive-depositors). The severity of the 2020 shock for financial-sector firms — where dividend smoothing broke down most sharply — is the market-choice counterpart documented in political-and-policy-uncertainty-and-payout. Dividend bans, capital, and credit supply The most forceful intervention is an outright ban, and the ECB's de facto COVID-19 dividend ban tests whether preserving buffers translates into credit. The ban's stated goal was to boost banks' capital to ensure credit supply, but because dividends matter to investors and banks might simply hoard the preserved buffers to boost payouts once the ban lifted, the effect on credit was a priori uncertain (sanders-2024-curse-and-blessing-the-effect-of-the-dividend). The announcement had a significantly negative impact on euro-area bank valuations — the "curse" — yet banks significantly expanded credit supply in the syndicated-loan market, with no counteracting effect from the negative stock-market reaction, a result corroborated in a within-loan setup exploiting the multi-bank nature of syndicated loans — the "blessing" (sanders-2024-curse-and-blessing-the-effect-of-the-dividend). The finding that curtailed payout can build usable capital echoes the post-crisis adjustment channel in which lower payouts and retained earnings fed capital ratios and, for better-capitalized banks, more lending (cohen-2016-banks-and-capital-requirements-channels-of-adjustment), and it operationalizes the externality logic under which unrestricted private payout is excessive from a sector-wide perspective (acharya-2017-bank-capital-and-dividend-externalities). Current assessment (2026-07): The crisis-era evidence points to a real trade-off in restricting bank payout — a measurable valuation cost against a capital-and-credit-supply benefit — but tilts toward restriction being worthwhile when externalities are strong and the alternative is distress-driven voluntary cuts. Mandated, system-wide restrictions carry a smaller equity-price penalty than individual distress-signaling cuts, and at least in the euro-area COVID episode the preserved buffers translated into expanded lending rather than being hoarded for post-ban payout (marsh-2023-supervisory-stringency-payout-restrictions-and-bank-equity-prices; sanders-2024-curse-and-blessing-the-effect-of-the-dividend; cohen-2016-banks-and-capital-requirements-channels-of-adjustment). What remains contested is the optimal design of such restrictions and how to weigh the valuation cost when the externality is weak. Open questions The unresolved core is how to reconcile the signaling and risk-shifting readings of the same distribution, since a crisis dividend can be both a costly signal of health to depositors and a transfer of residual risk to creditors (forti-2015-bank-dividends-and-signaling-to-information-sensitive-depositors; pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from). If risk-shifting dominates for distressed banks while signaling dominates for healthy ones, the value of payout — and the case for restricting it — becomes state-contingent, and the empirical challenge is separating the two in the same cross-section (pugachev-2022-the-risk-shifting-value-of-payout-evidence-from; tripathy-2021-dividends-and-financial-health-evidence-from-us-bank). A second open question is the optimal design of payout restrictions given the externality: if bank capital is a public good whose private provision is deficient, the efficient policy internalizes the cross-bank spillover, but how to calibrate restrictions to the strength of interconnection without imposing needless valuation costs on well-capitalized banks is unsettled (acharya-2017-bank-capital-and-dividend-externalities; marsh-2023-supervisory-stringency-payout-restrictions-and-bank-equity-prices). Whether inside-debt-style incentive alignment could substitute for direct restriction — disciplining risk-shifting through compensation rather than supervision — is a further design margin the evidence only begins to address (srivastav-2014-ceo-inside-debt-holdings-and-risk-shifting-evidence). pages.text: International Evidence on Dividends Cross-country research is where the dividend literature turns the fixed institutional backdrop of a single market into a set of variables. Within one country the level of investor protection, the tax regime, and the typical ownership structure are constants, so a determinant of payout cannot be separated from the institutions that surround it; exploiting variation across nations in law, taxation, ownership, and disclosure makes those constants into regressors and turns cross-country data into the natural laboratory for testing dividend theory. The organizing insight of this literature, from La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny, is that dividends are shaped by how well legal regimes protect minority shareholders — the "outcome" versus "substitute" framing that anchors the entire body of work and whose master variable is the common-law/civil-law divide of legal origin. Around this axis the field integrates evidence on the lifecycle determinants of paying, tax regimes, ownership concentration and expropriation, disclosure and earnings quality, dividend smoothing, catering, and the worldwide decline in the propensity to pay. The recurring payoff is a verdict on which US-based "puzzles" replicate globally and which are regime-specific: agency and lifecycle explanations travel, whereas signaling, catering, and disappearing dividends turn out to be conditional on the legal environment. The legal-origin thread runs through every sub-theme below rather than sitting in a section of its own. The legal-origin / investor-protection axis The foundational test pits two agency models of dividends against each other. Under the outcome model, dividends are paid because minority shareholders with legal power pressure insiders to disgorge cash, so stronger minority rights predict higher payouts; under the substitute model, insiders who expect to return to equity markets pay dividends to build a reputation for fair treatment, so stronger rights predict lower payouts (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). The cross-section of roughly 4,000 companies from 33 countries with differing minority-rights regimes supports the outcome model: better-protected shareholders extract more, not less (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). This makes legal origin — the common-law regimes that tend to protect minorities strongly versus the civil-law regimes that protect them weakly — the master variable of the field, and it recurs as an interaction term throughout later work on taxation, disclosure, catering, and the propensity to pay (alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends; ferris-2009-catering-effects-in-corporate-dividend-policy-the-international; brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). The long-run record adds a note of caution about how forcefully the axis operates through legislative change: across all Belgian firms listed in Brussels over 1838–2012 — a period spanning very weak pre-WWI protection, its gradual improvement, and the 1920 introduction of dividend taxation — dividend policy is remarkably stable and changes in investor-protection and tax legislation had little impact, suggesting the cross-sectional protection–payout link need not translate into strong within-country time-series responses to legal reform (moortgat-2017-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividend-policy-long-run). Cross-paper pattern: The cross-country evidence converges on the outcome model — stronger minority-shareholder protection is associated with higher payout — with legal origin (common vs. civil law) as the organizing axis, though the long-run Belgian record shows the association is weaker as a within-country response to legislative change than as a cross-sectional regularity (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality; moortgat-2017-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividend-policy-long-run). Lifecycle and the determinants of paying The most robustly replicated cross-country regularity is the lifecycle pattern of who pays. Across the US, Canada, UK, Germany, France, and Japan, the propensity to pay dividends is higher among larger and more profitable firms and those for which retained earnings make up a large fraction of total equity — the earned/contributed-capital signature of the lifecycle theory (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). The worldwide-decline study reaches the same cross-sectional verdict in a far larger sample of more than 17,000 firms from 33 countries: larger firms, more profitable firms, and firms with low growth opportunities are more likely to pay (fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). The lifecycle account is not merely mechanical maturity; it carries an agency component that the disclosure environment activates, so that the earned/contributed-capital pattern holds around the world and the firm's disclosure environment shapes payout through its effect on agency costs — an agency-cost-inclusive lifecycle theory (brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). The lifecycle determinants also survive controlling for the cash-flow-uncertainty channel that operates worldwide, underscoring that maturity and risk are distinct forces (see the uncertainty treatment in financial-flexibility-and-payout). This convergence is what lets the international record be read as support for agency/lifecycle theories where it casts doubt on signaling and catering (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). Cross-paper pattern: Size, profitability, and a high earned/contributed-capital (retained-earnings) mix are the robust global determinants of the propensity to pay, replicating across six developed markets and 33-country samples, with the disclosure environment adding an agency-cost overlay (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on; fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence; brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). Taxation across regimes Cross-country variation in tax systems exposes how the dividend/repurchase channel choice responds to the tax wedge, and it does so interacted with investor protection rather than uniformly. Under a classical tax system, firms in strong-investor-protection countries pay lower cash dividends than firms in weak-protection countries but repurchase more shares to maximize shareholders' after-tax returns — the reverse of the naive protection–payout prediction once the tax cost of cash dividends is admitted (alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends). In weak-protection countries both cash dividends and repurchases are low and less responsive to taxes: protected investors weigh the tax cost of dividends against the agency-cost benefit of disgorgement and shift toward repurchases, while unprotected investors accept whatever they can extract even at high tax cost (alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends). This tax–protection interaction refines rather than overturns the outcome model, and it connects to the lifecycle determinants because the earned-capital firms most likely to pay are also those with the flexibility to substitute repurchases for dividends (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). The long-run Belgian evidence again tempers expectations about the time-series force of taxation: the 1920 introduction of dividend taxation left dividend policy largely unmoved, so the strong cross-sectional tax responsiveness is not mirrored by a sharp response to the arrival of a tax (moortgat-2017-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividend-policy-long-run). Tax regimes also condition specific event-driven results, such as the imputation-versus-classical contrast in how carbon risk affects payout, treated in political-and-policy-uncertainty-and-payout. Ownership, expropriation, and weak institutions Where ownership is concentrated and external institutions are weak, dividends take on a role as a substitute for the institutional protections that are missing. Concentrated controlling shareholders can expropriate minority investors, and the value of the cash the firm holds falls accordingly: the relation between cash holdings and firm value is much weaker in poor-investor-protection countries, consistent with controlling shareholders extracting private benefits from retained cash, and the relation between dividends and firm value is itself weaker where protection is stronger (pinkowitz-2006-does-the-contribution-of-corporate-cash-holdings-and; laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world). In this setting firms use the timing and commitment of payout as a bonding device: in weak-institution countries firms display a higher speed of adjustment to their target payout ratio, pay dividends earlier in the lifecycle, and are more likely to disclose a policy committing to pay a minimum percentage of earnings — a commitment that reveals the extent of firm-level agency conflict to future investors and facilitates raising external capital (ellahie-2021-show-me-the-money-dividend-policy-in-countries). Within weak-institution countries, the firms with the highest-speed-of-adjustment policies have fewer agency problems and greater ability to raise capital, and their earnings announcements draw larger market reactions — evidence that the payout commitment is read as informative precisely where institutions cannot be relied on (ellahie-2021-show-me-the-money-dividend-policy-in-countries). The same logic underlies the earnings-quality results: payers manage earnings less to establish credible reputations and ease access to external funds, and the effect is strongest where institutions are weak (he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries). Cross-border regulatory cooperation can substitute for domestic institutional reform in the same vein: firms cross-listed in the U.S. from countries that joined the Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU) securities-enforcement arrangement showed significant post-entry increases in dividend payouts, with effects concentrated in high-agency-cost firms from countries with weak external governance and opaque disclosure — consistent with strengthened cross-border enforcement reducing expropriation and supporting the outcome model even absent domestic legal change (chen-2022-cross-border-enforcement-of-securities-laws-and-dividend-payouts). Disclosure, transparency, and earnings quality The information environment is a cross-country moderator in its own right, and it carries the outcome-versus-substitute tension into the disclosure domain. The outcome hypothesis predicts that transparent disclosure raises payout because shareholders can more accurately measure and demand excess cash; the substitute hypothesis predicts that opaque disclosure raises payout because managers have stronger incentives to build a fair-treatment reputation — and the international disclosure evidence confirms both, delivering the agency-cost-inclusive lifecycle theory in which disclosure shapes payout through agency costs (brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). Earnings quality moves in tandem: across 23,429 firms from 29 countries, dividend payers manage earnings less than non-payers, and the gap is stronger in countries with weak investor protection and high opacity, with payers managing earnings even less when they issue equity following dividends — a pattern most pronounced in weak-institution, low-transparency settings (he-2017-dividend-policy-and-earnings-management-across-countries). The interpretation is that firms pair dividends with cleaner earnings to establish credible reputations and facilitate external financing, which dovetails with the commitment mechanism in weak-institution countries and with the tax–protection interaction, since disclosure quality and protection tend to co-move with legal origin (ellahie-2021-show-me-the-money-dividend-policy-in-countries; alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends). Disclosure thus operates as the informational face of the same investor-protection axis that governs the level of payout. Dividend smoothing across countries Lintner-style smoothing, long treated as a near-universal fact of dividend policy, turns out to vary systematically with institutions once the cross-country lens is applied. Across more than two thousand firms from 24 countries, managers of firms with low market-to-book ratios and less cash smooth dividends more, consistent with both agency and asymmetric-information motives operating simultaneously (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). Institutions shape the degree of smoothing in interpretable directions: firms with highly concentrated ownership and strong corporate governance smooth less — because the monitoring or control that concentration and governance provide substitutes for the commitment role smoothing otherwise plays — while firms in highly competitive industries smooth more (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). Beyond firm characteristics, the extent of legal protection, the tax regime, and national culture add explanatory power, so smoothing is jointly an agency, information, legal, and cultural phenomenon rather than a mechanical Lintner constant (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing). The cultural dimension is corroborated by behavioural evidence: a mental-accounting model relating payout to patience, loss aversion, and ambiguity aversion is verified across 29 countries and more than 43,000 firm-years, establishing behavioural patterns as direct determinants of dividend policy that earlier work could only reach indirectly (breuer-2014-the-behavioral-foundations-of-corporate-dividend-policy-a). Language structure adds yet another layer: firms in markets using languages with a weak future-time-reference (FTR) — where the grammar does not require speakers to distinguish present from future events (e.g., Chinese, Japanese, German) — pay systematically lower dividends than firms in strong-FTR markets (e.g., French, Italian), because weak-FTR speakers perceive future dividends as nearer and value them more highly, reducing the preference for immediate payout. Within-market quasi-experiments (Hong Kong after the 1997 sovereignty handover; German- vs. French-speaking Swiss regions) confirm the causal direction and show the effect is not driven by co-varying legal or institutional differences (he-zhang-2022-languages-and-dividends). Regional social trust offers a further regime-contingent cultural signal: in China's weak-institution environment, firms in low-trust regions pay higher dividends than those in high-trust regions, because low trust amplifies agency conflicts and shareholders demand dividends as a governance substitute — a pattern that inverts the positive trust–dividend relationship found in the U.S. where formal institutions are strong and trust reinforces shareholder confidence, with the direction of the relationship depending on the quality of the surrounding formal institutional backdrop (qin-2022-social-trust-and-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-china). Smoothing and its cultural determinants connect to the measurement tradition catalogued in lintner-model-and-smoothing-measures. Catering and the worldwide decline in paying Two prominent US findings — catering to a time-varying dividend premium, and the disappearance of dividends — are the sharpest cases of regime-conditionality. Dividend catering is present among firms in common-law countries but not among firms in civil-law countries, and it persists after controlling for firm lifecycle, so the catering channel operates only where the legal regime and its investor protections let shareholders both force dividends from managers and bid up the price of payers (ferris-2009-catering-effects-in-corporate-dividend-policy-the-international). Civil-law firms' relative failure to cater may reflect controlling shareholders' consumption of private benefits or indifference to temporary market misvaluation of their equity (ferris-2009-catering-effects-in-corporate-dividend-policy-the-international). The disappearing-dividends phenomenon is similarly uneven: there is a significant worldwide decline in the propensity to pay, driven mostly by smaller, less profitable firms with more investment opportunities, and it persists after controlling for firm characteristics — yet the decline in mean payout ratios and in the proportion of payers is much more pronounced in civil-law countries (fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). Denis and Osobov sharpen the contrast further: outside the US there is little evidence of a systematic positive relation between the relative prices of payers and non-payers and the propensity to pay, aggregate dividends have not declined, and abandonment by existing payers is economically unimportant except in Japan — findings that cast doubt on signaling, clientele, and catering explanations while supporting agency/lifecycle theories (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). Cross-paper pattern: Catering and disappearing dividends are legal-origin-conditional — catering appears in common-law but not civil-law regimes, and the propensity-to-pay decline is concentrated in civil-law countries — so both US "puzzles" are properties of the legal environment rather than universal features of payout (ferris-2009-catering-effects-in-corporate-dividend-policy-the-international; fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence; denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). What replicates and what is US-specific Read as a whole, the international record functions as the strongest available test of competing dividend theories because it can hold up each theory against variation the US alone cannot supply. The agency and lifecycle accounts travel: the size/profitability/earned-capital determinants of paying replicate across developed and broad multi-country samples, the outcome model of protection and payout holds cross-sectionally, and the agency-cost-inclusive lifecycle theory is confirmed through the disclosure channel (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on; laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; brockman-2011-earned-contributed-capital-dividend-policy-and-disclosure-quality). By contrast the signaling, clientele, and catering explanations are regime-conditional: catering is confined to common-law countries, the price–propensity relation that would evidence catering or signaling is largely absent outside the US, and the disappearing-dividends trend is a civil-law phenomenon (ferris-2009-catering-effects-in-corporate-dividend-policy-the-international; denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on; fatemi-2012-yes-dividends-are-disappearing-worldwide-evidence). Even smoothing, the most Lintnerian of stylized facts, is conditional on ownership, governance, legal protection, tax, and culture rather than universal (javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing; breuer-2014-the-behavioral-foundations-of-corporate-dividend-policy-a). Current assessment (2026-07): The cross-country literature has largely settled that the agency/lifecycle theory is the robust global account of why firms pay, with investor protection (the outcome model) as its institutional master variable, while signaling, catering, and the disappearing-dividends trend are conditional on legal origin rather than universal. The tax channel refines the outcome model — strong-protection firms substitute repurchases for taxed dividends — and disclosure, ownership, and culture enter as moderators of the same protection axis. New evidence expands the cultural channel: language structure (future-time-reference) and regional social trust each carry residual explanatory power for dividend levels after controlling for legal indices, and their direction of effect on payout reverses depending on whether formal institutions are strong or weak — pointing to the quality of formal institutions as the variable that determines whether informal mechanisms amplify or substitute for governance pressure. Cross-border securities-enforcement cooperation (MMoU) produces payout effects analogous to domestic legal reform, and comply-or-explain regulations achieve mechanical payout compliance at measurable financing costs, both suggesting that the form and credibility of the enforcement mechanism matter as much as the existence of the statute. The open frontier is the endogeneity of institutions and the separation of culture from law, and how to reconcile forceful cross-sectional effects with the near-stability of dividend policy in long-run within-country records (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends; moortgat-2017-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividend-policy-long-run; he-zhang-2022-languages-and-dividends; qin-2022-social-trust-and-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-china). Open questions The central unresolved problem is the endogeneity of institutions: legal origin, investor protection, tax regime, ownership structure, and disclosure quality are correlated with one another and with unobserved features of economic development, so isolating the causal contribution of any one is hard even with 33-country cross-sections (laporta-2000-agency-problems-and-dividend-policies-around-the-world; alzahrani-2012-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividends). Distinguishing culture from law is a related open question, since the behavioural determinants — patience, loss aversion, ambiguity aversion — and the legal-protection variables both track legal origin and both carry explanatory power for smoothing and payout (breuer-2014-the-behavioral-foundations-of-corporate-dividend-policy-a; javakhadze-2014-an-international-analysis-of-dividend-smoothing); language structure (FTR) and regional social trust now add further informal channels that do not reduce to the protection index but co-vary with it, sharpening the separation problem (he-zhang-2022-languages-and-dividends; qin-2022-social-trust-and-dividend-payouts-evidence-from-china). The effectiveness of regulatory design is a third open question: the comply-or-explain experience in China shows that minimum-payout targets can achieve compliance while degrading firm value and forcing debt issuance, raising the question of when mandatory payout rules protect minorities versus distort investment (he-li-2018-the-effects-of-a-comply-or-explain-dividend-regulation-in-china). Finally, the long-run and modern records must be reconciled: modern cross-country panels show strong protection and tax effects, yet the 1838–2012 Belgian evidence shows dividend policy barely responding to sweeping changes in investor protection and the introduction of taxation, raising the question of whether the cross-sectional associations reflect slow-moving equilibrium selection rather than responsiveness to institutional change (moortgat-2017-investor-protection-taxation-and-dividend-policy-long-run). headings: Black's dividend puzzle and the frictions that resolve it
A natural experiment on the frictions
pages.excerpt: The theoretical spine of the payout literature is the Miller–Modigliani (1961) proposition that, in a frictionless capital market and holding investment policy fixed, the division of earnings between distribution and retention cannot affect firm value — investors can costlessly…
pages.text: MM Irrelevance and the Payout Puzzles The theoretical spine of the payout literature is the Miller–Modigliani (1961) proposition that, in a frictionless capital market and holding investment policy fixed, the division of earnings between distribution and retention cannot affect firm value — investors can costlessly undo any payout choice through "homemade dividends." This irrelevance result is a benchmark, not a description of the world, and its enduring role is to force every positive theory of payout to name the specific friction it relaxes. Around that benchmark accreted a family of puzzles: Fischer Black's dividend puzzle (why pay taxed dividends at all?), the disappearing-dividends puzzle (why did payers vanish and then partly return?), and the substitution puzzle (what does the displacement of dividends by repurchases imply for irrelevance?). This page synthesizes how each friction — taxes, information asymmetry, agency costs, transaction costs, and the mere feasibility of retention — converts the irrelevance baseline into a determinate positive theory, and how a modern reappraisal of the theorem itself has reframed what MM does and does not claim. It carries no frontier section: its scope is foundational. The irrelevance benchmark The MM logic rests on a separation: given a fixed investment program, the funds distributed today must be replaced by funds raised tomorrow (or forgone consumption financed by asset sales), so a shareholder indifferent to the timing of consumption can replicate any payout stream by trading on personal account. The homemade-dividend argument makes this precise: a shareholder who wants more cash than the firm distributes can sell a fraction of her holding, while one who wants less can reinvest the dividend, so that for a fixed investment policy the value $V_0$ equals the present value of the underlying project cash flows and is invariant to how those flows are split between a dividend $D_t$ and reinvestment. Value therefore depends on the earning power of assets, not on the packaging of the returns. The literature treats this as the correct point of departure while disagreeing sharply on what it licenses. The most influential reappraisal grants the algebra but denies the interpretation, arguing that MM's frictionless setup does not actually address the value comparison MM themselves posed (deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem). A reconciling treatment accepts MM's perfect-market result as valid within its assumptions and locates the disagreement in what happens once repurchases and agency costs enter (handley-2008-dividend-policy-reconciling-dd-with-mm). The benchmark also has an empirical corollary that survives the theoretical dispute: managers behave as though distribution matters, treating the dividend level as on par with investment decisions rather than as a residual (brav-2005-payout-policy-in-the-21st-century). The value of the benchmark is diagnostic rather than descriptive — because it specifies the one world in which payout cannot matter, it turns the empirical question "why does payout appear to matter?" into the sharper question "which of MM's assumptions fails here?" Every downstream theory in the collection can be located by the assumption it relaxes: signaling relaxes symmetric information, agency theory relaxes the assumption that managers maximize shareholder value, clientele and catering models relax the frictionless-trading and rational-pricing assumptions, and the lifecycle account relaxes the assumption that retention is costless. The DeAngelo–DeAngelo critique The sharpest challenge holds that the theorem is "irrelevant" in a double sense. The argument is that the joint effect of MM's assumptions is to mandate 100% free-cash-flow payout in every period: because retention that earns only the market rate creates no value and the assumptions foreclose value-destroying retention, "niggardly payouts" are infeasible and the firm's opportunity set is artificially constrained to policies that fully distribute free cash flow. Irrelevance then obtains, but in an economically vacuous sense, since the interesting comparison — generous versus niggardly payout — has been assumed away. Once the assumptions are relaxed to allow retention, payout policy matters in exactly the same sense that investment policy does (deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem). The critique carries several constructive claims: the standard Fisherian model is empirically refutable and predicts that firms make large payouts in present-value terms; the present value of distributions equals the PV of project cash flows only when payout is optimized; and the NPV rule for investment is necessary but not sufficient for value maximization, requiring an analogous rule for payout. The verbal, logical character of this critique — it introduces no new formal model — is worth stressing, and the reconciling literature engages it on exactly those terms (handley-2008-dividend-policy-reconciling-dd-with-mm). Reconciling the two views The reconciliation turns on two devices the original irrelevance statement underweights: stock repurchases and agency costs. Repurchases restore a channel through which a firm can distribute free cash flow without committing to a permanent dividend, which addresses the DeAngelo–DeAngelo insistence that full distribution be feasible; agency costs supply the reason retention is not value-neutral in practice, since cash left inside the firm can be diverted or wasted (handley-2008-dividend-policy-reconciling-dd-with-mm). On this reading MM's result and the DeAngelo–DeAngelo critique are not contradictory but describe different opportunity sets: perfect-market irrelevance holds within MM's assumptions, while payout relevance emerges the moment retention and its agency consequences are admitted (deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem). Survey evidence is consistent with the reconciled picture: managers use repurchases as the flexible outlet for residual cash after investment while guarding the dividend as a commitment, and they express only weak support for the agency, signaling, and clientele stories in their pure forms (brav-2005-payout-policy-in-the-21st-century). The reconciliation matters beyond exegesis, because the two devices it introduces are exactly the ones that anchor the modern positive theory of payout: agency costs supply the free-cash-flow motive that the lifecycle literature builds on, and repurchases supply the flexible channel whose growth generated the substitution and disappearing-dividends puzzles treated below. In this sense the reconciliation is less a truce between two papers than the hinge connecting the frictionless benchmark to the whole empirical edifice — every friction-based theory can be read as specifying which of MM's assumptions it relaxes and what value consequence follows. The reconciliation matters for the field's self-image: if the two views were genuinely contradictory, the whole "MM plus a friction" research program would rest on an incoherent foundation, whereas if they describe different opportunity sets, the program is secure and the DeAngelo–DeAngelo critique becomes a clarification of scope rather than a refutation. Cross-paper pattern: The MM/DeAngelo–DeAngelo standoff dissolves once repurchases (a feasible full-distribution channel) and agency costs (a reason retention is not value-neutral) are added — the two devices Handley identifies as the reconciling mechanisms (handley-2008-dividend-policy-reconciling-dd-with-mm; deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem; brav-2005-payout-policy-in-the-21st-century). Black's dividend puzzle and the frictions that resolve it Black's puzzle — why firms pay dividends that were, historically, taxed more heavily than capital gains — presupposes that a value-maximizing firm should not pay them, and each candidate friction offers a different resolution. The critique above dissolves the puzzle at its root, arguing that it is a "non-puzzle" because it rests on the mistaken idea that MM's irrelevance theorem applies to payout/retention decisions, which it does not (deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem). The empirical literatures then test which friction actually binds. Survey evidence weakly supports agency, signaling, and clientele motives and relegates taxes to a secondary role (brav-2005-payout-policy-in-the-21st-century); international evidence discriminates in favour of agency-cost lifecycle explanations and against signaling, clientele, and catering (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on); and a historical experiment that strips away taxes, regulation, and institutional owners finds the surviving motive to be information-communication rather than agency, illiquidity, catering, or behavioural stories (turner-2013-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-evidence-from-an). That the resolutions differ by setting is itself informative: no single friction explains payout everywhere, which is why the puzzle spawned a family of theories rather than one winner. Evidence from comprehensive Swedish firm-owner data refines the taxes-versus-other-frictions question by measuring how tax sensitivity interacts with agency and coordination frictions, rather than treating taxes as either primary or secondary in isolation. Absent frictions — in wholly owned closely held corporations where a single owner-manager faces aligned incentives — a dividend tax cut of roughly seven percentage points caused owner-managers to increase the dividend share of compensation by about 7.3 percentage points (a 69% rise relative to the pre-reform average), confirming that taxes have a first-order impact on payout in a nearly friction-free environment. But as agency issues and shareholder conflicts increase, this sensitivity is sharply muted: in firms with three owners, the response is 40% smaller; once a firm has five or more owners, the tax effect is negligible. Three mechanisms account for the attenuation: coordination costs among shareholders, heterogeneity in owners' tax preferences, and separation of ownership and control (jacob-michaely-2017-taxation-and-dividend-policy-the-muting-effect-of-agency-iss). The result reframes Black's puzzle: taxes are a powerful force on payout when uncorrupted by other frictions, but the interaction of ownership dispersion and agency costs explains why the tax channel appears secondary in survey and cross-sectional studies that capture the full, friction-ridden population of firms. The disappearing-dividends puzzle The secular collapse in the fraction of dividend payers poses a distinct challenge to any value-based theory: if paying maximizes value for the right firms, why did so many stop? The founding decomposition shows the fall from 66.5% of firms in 1978 to 20.8% in 1999 owes partly to a firm population increasingly tilted toward small, unprofitable, high-growth new listings, but also to a genuine drop in propensity that holds regardless of characteristics and is at least as important as the compositional shift (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). The puzzle deepened and then partly resolved with the reappearance after 2000: a later decomposition attributes half the original disappearance to characteristics and half to proclivity, and 82% of the reappearance to higher proclivity among stable, profitable firms, while noting that newly listed and delisted firms — not initiations and omissions by continuing firms — drive the trends (michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). Crucially, that same study finds the disappearance of total payout is far smaller and shorter-lived than the disappearance of dividends, pointing directly to substitution between dividends and repurchases (michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends). The measurement questions underlying these decompositions are treated at payout-ratio-and-propensity-to-pay. What makes the disappearance a genuine puzzle rather than a mere fact is its tension with the lifecycle logic: if the pay decision tracks the earned/contributed capital mix and firm maturity, a wave of young, contributed-capital-heavy listings mechanically lowers the payer fraction without any firm changing its behaviour, yet the residual propensity decline shows that behaviour changed too (fama-2001-disappearing-dividends-changing-firm-characteristics-or-lower-propensity). International evidence complicates the "puzzle" framing further: outside the US aggregate dividends never declined and remained concentrated among the largest, most profitable firms, with any propensity dip driven by newly listed firms failing to initiate rather than by existing payers abandoning dividends (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). The puzzle is thus partly an artefact of the unit of analysis — firm counts versus aggregate dollars — a point the measurement page develops. The substitution puzzle If repurchases have displaced dividends, then the "disappearance" may be a change of form rather than a change of substance — which bears directly on whether MM's irrelevance-of-form survives. The substitution hypothesis holds that firms finance repurchases with funds that would otherwise have raised dividends, so repurchases became the preferred vehicle for initiating a cash payout even as established firms preserved their dividends (grullon-2002-dividends-share-repurchases-and-the-substitution-hypothesis). By the late 2000s repurchases were the dominant payout form, dividend-only firms had become largely extinct, and the overall level of repurchases remained fundamentally anchored to earnings (skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). The taxonomy that emerged — firms that pay dividends and repurchase regularly, firms that only repurchase regularly, and firms that repurchase occasionally — implies that "the payout decision" is really two decisions, a commitment margin and a flexible margin, and only the former resembles the sticky dividend of the mid-century literature (skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). The decisive reframing is that on a net-cash-distribution basis the decline vanishes: contrary to the dividend evidence, the conditional propensity to distribute net cash to equity holders has not declined over three decades, and net payout yields have actually risen (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined). This is the empirical fulcrum of the whole puzzle — it suggests total-payout relevance while leaving the irrelevance of the dividend/repurchase split an open possibility. It also inverts the apparent challenge to value theory: rather than firms retreating from distribution in a way a value-based account would struggle to explain, they substituted a more flexible channel for a rigid one while holding total returns to equity roughly constant, which is exactly what a friction-augmented MM model — repurchases feasible, retention costly through agency — would predict (grullon-2002-dividends-share-repurchases-and-the-substitution-hypothesis; grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined). Cross-paper pattern: Measured as net cash to equity, aggregate payout did not fall — net payout yields rose while dividend incidence dropped — a stability that Grullon–Michaely, the later reappearance decomposition, and the earnings-anchored repurchase evidence all converge on (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined; michaely-2022-disappearing-and-reappearing-dividends; skinner-2008-the-evolving-relation-between-earnings-dividends-and-stock). A natural experiment on the frictions Because the competing resolutions of Black's puzzle differ by institutional setting, a market that mechanically shuts off some frictions functions as a discriminating test. The Victorian London market between 1825 and 1870 had effectively zero tax rates, an unregulated capital market, and no institutional stockholders, allowing those determinants to be ruled out ex ante; in that setting share repurchases — though legal — were not used to return cash, and the evidence supports the information-communication explanation for dividends while offering little support for agency, illiquidity, catering, or behavioural accounts (turner-2013-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-evidence-from-an). This complements the contemporary cross-country test, which reaches a different verdict — favouring agency-cost lifecycle theories over signaling, clientele, and catering in modern developed markets (denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). Read together, the two suggest the binding friction is not fixed across institutional environments, which is precisely why the puzzles have proven durable rather than decisively solved. Open questions and cross-links The unresolved core is the status of irrelevance-of-form against the relevance of total payout. The net-payout evidence establishes that firms have not reduced what they return, only how they package it, which leaves open whether the dividend/repurchase mix is itself value-relevant or a matter of clientele and flexibility with no first-order effect on value (grullon-2011-has-the-propensity-to-pay-out-declined; grullon-2002-dividends-share-repurchases-and-the-substitution-hypothesis). A second open question is how far the DeAngelo–DeAngelo reframing should propagate through applied work that still invokes "irrelevance" loosely: if payout is relevant "in exactly the same sense that investment policy is," then the necessary condition for value maximization is a payout rule as well as an NPV rule, and empirical models that treat distribution as a pure residual are misspecified (deangelo-2006-the-irrelevance-of-the-mm-dividend-irrelevance-theorem; handley-2008-dividend-policy-reconciling-dd-with-mm). A third is whether the frictions that resolve Black's puzzle are stable across time and place or genuinely regime-dependent: the divergence between the Victorian information-communication verdict and the modern agency-lifecycle verdict suggests the binding friction shifts with the institutional environment, so that a single universal resolution to the dividend puzzle may not exist (turner-2013-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-evidence-from-an; denis-2008-why-do-firms-pay-dividends-international-evidence-on). These questions matter because nearly every other page in this wiki inherits a stance on them: the signaling, agency, catering, and clientele pages are each a claim about which friction converts the baseline into a positive theory. Current assessment (2026-07): The field's working consensus is that MM irrelevance survives as a benchmark and total-payout relevance is well established, but the irrelevance of the dividend-versus-repurchase form remains genuinely unsettled — the net-payout evidence is consistent both with pure form-neutrality and with form-relevance driven by flexibility and clientele frictions that the abstract-level evidence here cannot separate. pages.title: Political and Policy Uncertainty and Payout
headings: Two rival responses: conserve versus disgorge
pages.excerpt: This page synthesizes the post-2015 wave of research on how macro-level and non-market uncertainty shapes corporate payout — economic policy uncertainty (EPU), political risk and crises, corruption, CEO political ideology, political freedom and democracy, pandemic shocks, and…
pages.text: Political and Policy Uncertainty and Payout This page synthesizes the post-2015 wave of research on how macro-level and non-market uncertainty shapes corporate payout — economic policy uncertainty (EPU), political risk and crises, corruption, CEO political ideology, political freedom and democracy, pandemic shocks, and climate and carbon risk. The literature poses one question with two rival answers: does heightened uncertainty lead firms to conserve cash — a precautionary, flexibility-preserving response that cuts or reshapes payout — or to disgorge cash — a shielding, agency-mitigating response that raises payout and signals commitment to outside investors? The record turns out to be genuinely two-sided: high EPU raises dividends in international data, while political crises, climate risk, and firm-level cash-flow uncertainty cut or shift payout. The reconciliation is that the sign is conditional — on the type of uncertainty, its horizon and reversibility, firm free cash flow, and the strength of country institutions. This is the frontier of the payout literature, extending the classical determinants of distribution (agency, signaling, taxes, lifecycle) to a new class of macro and non-market risks that became salient after the global financial crisis and COVID-19. The sections below set up the conserve-versus-disgorge tension, then work through the uncertainty classes: economic policy uncertainty, political risk and corruption, political freedom and democracy, CEO ideology, the COVID-19 shock, and climate and carbon risk, before turning to reconciliation. Two rival responses: conserve versus disgorge The organizing tension is between two logics that predict opposite payout responses to the same rise in uncertainty. The precautionary/flexibility logic holds that when the future becomes less predictable and external financing more costly, firms retain cash — cutting payout or shifting it toward reversible forms — to preserve the option to invest and to avoid distress. The shielding/agency logic holds the reverse: where uncertainty raises the risk that insiders, controlling shareholders, or a predatory environment will expropriate cash, firms distribute more to remove cash from harm's way and to mitigate agency conflict. The international EPU evidence sits on the disgorge side, reading high-uncertainty dividends as an agency-mitigation device (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence); the political-crisis evidence sits on the conserve side, reading dividend termination as precautionary (huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international); and the corruption evidence adds a distinct geographic "shielding" channel in which a more predatory local environment raises payout (hossain-2021-political-corruption-and-corporate-payouts). The tension is not merely definitional — it forces the field to specify scope conditions rather than a single sign, and the moderators that flip it are free cash flow, governance, and country-level protection (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence; huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international). Cross-paper pattern: Uncertainty does not have a single sign on payout. It raises distribution where the dominant threat is expropriation of retained cash (EPU as agency-mitigation, corruption as shielding) and lowers or reshapes it where the dominant threat is a costly future funding shortfall (political crises, climate risk, cash-flow uncertainty). Free cash flow, governance, and institutional protection are the conditions that determine which force dominates (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence; huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international; hossain-2021-political-corruption-and-corporate-payouts). Economic policy uncertainty Economic policy uncertainty — the unpredictability of governments' fiscal, regulatory, and monetary policy — is the most directly measured of the macro channels, and the first international evidence establishes a positive sign. Across 19 countries, a high level of EPU is positively associated with dividend payout, robust to alternative payout measures, to controlling for other sources of uncertainty, and to addressing endogeneity (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence). The interpretation is agency-mitigating: dividends help discipline the use of cash during high-EPU periods, and consistent with this the effect is moderated by firms' free cash flow and governance quality and by the country-level quality of shareholder protection, disclosure, enforcement, and creditor protection (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence). A tax-policy natural experiment supplies a complementary but distinct mechanism at the U.S. level: facing uncertainty around individual dividend-tax increases scheduled for 2011 and 2013, firms time the tax environment, initiating or intensively raising dividends one year before an expected increase, and — when uncertainty is lower in 2012 — favouring special dividends over commitment to regular ones (buchanan-2017-uncertainty-and-firm-dividend-policy-a-natural-experiment). The response is strongest in firms with high tax-affected ownership, supporting a "prepare for the worst" reading in which firms act to protect shareholders from an anticipated adverse policy shift (buchanan-2017-uncertainty-and-firm-dividend-policy-a-natural-experiment). The two studies together show that EPU's positive payout effect can arise from both agency-mitigation and tax-timing, and that the special-versus-regular dividend margin is itself a flexibility lever, connecting to financial-flexibility-and-payout. A related margin is the risk-transfer response: facing higher EPU, firms increase pension underfunding — shifting risk onto employees — and the effect is stronger for high-dividend-paying firms, suggesting that some firms preserve payout under uncertainty precisely by offloading risk elsewhere (cumming-2024-are-companies-offloading-risk-onto-employees-in-times). Political risk, crises, and corruption Acute political risk pulls in the opposite direction from EPU, toward conservation. In a 35-country sample over 1990–2008, global political crises raise the market-perceived uncertainty and the cost of external financing, and using crisis events as a proxy for political risk, past dividend payers are more likely to terminate dividends and non-payers less likely to initiate them during high-political-risk periods — a precautionary response to political shocks (huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international). The effect is stronger for multinational corporations, whose exposure spans jurisdictions, but is attenuated by stabilizing institutions such as more stable political systems and stronger investor legal protection (huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international). Corruption operates through a different logic and yields the opposite sign: firms headquartered in more corrupt U.S. states pay out more to shareholders, a result robust to propensity-score matching, instrumental variables, headquarters relocations, and quasi-natural experiments, and interpreted as a geographic shielding channel in which distributing cash removes it from a predatory local environment (hossain-2021-political-corruption-and-corporate-payouts). The contrast is instructive: a discrete, potentially severe funding shock (a political crisis) triggers conservation, while a chronic expropriation-risk environment (corruption) triggers disgorgement — the same "non-market risk" heading, opposite payout responses, discriminated by whether the dominant threat is to future funding or to the safety of retained cash. Country institutions moderate both, linking this material to international-evidence-on-dividends and the investor-protection-and-payout debate. Political freedom, democracy, and institutions At the level of country political institutions, the evidence again points toward disgorgement in worse environments but distinguishes the value of that payout. Firms in less politically free countries pay out more cash, consistent with low political freedom marking a less friendly investment environment; firms reduce payouts when a country's political freedom improves, and pay out past excess cash while cutting future investment when political freedom deteriorates (guedhami-2017-political-freedom-and-corporate-payouts). Critically, this higher payout in less-free countries is not mainly an agency-easing device: the cash payouts there are more volatile and hence less valuable, undercutting a clean disgorgement reading (guedhami-2017-political-freedom-and-corporate-payouts). Democracy sharpens the picture from the other side. Across 18,410 firms in 63 countries over 1991–2018, and using instrumental variables, democracy improves dividends, with the effect more pronounced for firms with high agency costs and in countries with weak legal protection for shareholders (bui-2025-democracy-dividends-and-corporate-valuation). Democracy-induced dividends are also capitalized at a higher rate — especially for high-growth firms — adding to corporate value beyond the premium associated with shareholder-rights-induced dividends (bui-2025-democracy-dividends-and-corporate-valuation). The two studies are not contradictory once the moderators are read carefully: political un-freedom is associated with more but lower-quality payout, while democratization raises payout that markets value more, both effects concentrated where agency costs and weak protection make dividends most useful as a commitment device. CEO political ideology Not all political variation is at the country level; CEO political ideology introduces a firm-level, manager-driven channel. Measuring ideology by CEOs' political donations across S&P 500 firms over 1997–2019, conservative CEOs are more likely to pay dividends and to make share repurchases, and pay higher dividends, financing the higher distributions by drawing down cash holdings and reducing capital and R&D expenditure (bayat-2025-ceo-political-ideology-and-payout-policy). Importantly, ideology does not explain dividend cuts: firms led by conservative CEOs exhibit dividend flexibility comparable to those led by other CEOs, so the ideology effect operates on the level and initiation of payout rather than on the willingness to reverse it — leaving the flexibility option intact (bayat-2025-ceo-political-ideology-and-payout-policy). The COVID-19 period exposes the same disposition under stress: facing the pandemic, conservative CEOs were more likely to meet dividend expectations while aggressively reducing labour costs — using temporary downsizing to avoid earnings losses and thereby distributing the pandemic's pain onto the workforce rather than onto shareholders (bayat-2025-the-impact-of-ceo-political-ideology-on-labor). This firm-level channel is analytically distinct from the country-level uncertainty variables: it shows that who decides payout under uncertainty matters alongside the institutional environment in which the decision is made, and that a preference for maintaining shareholder distributions can be satisfied by shifting risk onto other stakeholders, echoing the pension-underfunding response (cumming-2024-are-companies-offloading-risk-onto-employees-in-times). The COVID-19 shock The COVID-19 pandemic is the cleanest acute uncertainty event in the corpus, and it produced a sharp precautionary response that broke the normal smoothing of dividends. For major equity markets, the proportion of index value attributable to the first five years of dividends dropped substantially in the first quarter of 2020, and the drop was not reversed by year-end — a durable breakdown of dividend smoothing rather than a transient dip (cejnek-2021-the-covid-19-pandemic-and-corporate-dividend-policy). The cross-section of who cut identifies the precautionary logic: the breakdown was less severe for firms with higher operating cash flows and more positively coskewed returns, and more pronounced for firms with higher leverage and in the financial sector; heavy dividend cutters also experienced a substantial increase in exposure to systematic risk (cejnek-2021-the-covid-19-pandemic-and-corporate-dividend-policy). The severity for financial firms links directly to the regulatory dividend restrictions treated in bank-payout-and-prudential-regulation, where the same event appears as a policy intervention rather than a firm choice. A dynamic-model rationalization is available from the flexibility literature: ambiguity aversion amplifies the precautionary motive and generates the elevated cash holdings and accelerated asset sales observed in the crisis (luo-2022-investment-payout-and-cash-management-under-risk-and via financial-flexibility-and-payout). The pandemic thus functions as a natural test of the conserve response — an unambiguous, severe, hard-to-reverse shock that pushed the cross-section toward cash retention in proportion to firms' exposure. Climate and carbon risk Climate risk is the slow-moving counterpart to the acute pandemic shock, and it elicits a distinctive reshaping rather than pure cutting of payout. Across 45 countries, firms in high-climate-risk countries reduce cash dividends but increasingly use share repurchases, substituting one channel for the other to raise payout flexibility in response to heightened climate risk (chang-2024-climate-risk-and-payout-flexibility-around-the-world). Operating volatility and financial constraints are the two channels through which climate risk operates, and the effect is stronger for firms more vulnerable to climate risk and in countries where people are more concerned about it and where the national culture emphasizes uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation (chang-2024-climate-risk-and-payout-flexibility-around-the-world). Carbon risk supplies quasi-experimental evidence with a tax-regime twist. In Australia's imputation environment, following ratification of the Kyoto Protocol the highest-emitting firms (polluters) reduce their probability of paying dividends and their payout ratio relative to non-polluters, and the reduction in payout ratio is smaller under the imputation system than under a classical tax system — highlighting that the tax environment conditions carbon risk's effect on payout level but not on the decision to pay (balachandran-2018-does-carbon-risk-matter-in-firm-dividend-policy). The post-Kyoto reduction is driven by polluters' relative increase in earnings uncertainty, giving carbon risk a clean causal route into payout via cash-flow uncertainty (balachandran-2018-does-carbon-risk-matter-in-firm-dividend-policy). Cross-paper pattern: Under both the acute COVID-19 shock and the slow-moving climate/carbon channel, the recurring response is a precautionary shift — cutting cash dividends (COVID, Kyoto polluters) or substituting reversible repurchases for committed dividends (climate risk) — that preserves flexibility rather than a wholesale exit from payout (cejnek-2021-the-covid-19-pandemic-and-corporate-dividend-policy; chang-2024-climate-risk-and-payout-flexibility-around-the-world; balachandran-2018-does-carbon-risk-matter-in-firm-dividend-policy). Open questions and reconciliation The central open question is when uncertainty raises versus cuts payout, and the emerging answer organizes the evidence by the nature of the threat rather than by a single elasticity. Country-level environments where the dominant risk is expropriation of retained cash — high EPU under weak governance, corruption, low political freedom — tend to raise payout as a shielding or agency-mitigation device (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence; hossain-2021-political-corruption-and-corporate-payouts; guedhami-2017-political-freedom-and-corporate-payouts). Acute, hard-to-reverse funding shocks where the dominant risk is a future shortfall — political crises, the pandemic, rising earnings uncertainty from carbon exposure — tend to cut or reshape payout toward reversible forms (huang-2015-political-risk-and-dividend-policy-evidence-from-international; cejnek-2021-the-covid-19-pandemic-and-corporate-dividend-policy; balachandran-2018-does-carbon-risk-matter-in-firm-dividend-policy). Whether the international EPU result survives a fully precautionary framework — that is, whether the positive sign is agency-mitigation or a composition effect of which firms pay under uncertainty — remains contested, and the moderating roles of horizon, reversibility, and institutions are still being mapped (attig-2021-dividends-and-economic-policy-uncertainty-international-evidence; chang-2024-climate-risk-and-payout-flexibility-around-the-world). Current assessment (2026-07): The field has moved from asking whether uncertainty affects payout to specifying which uncertainty and under what conditions. The best-supported reconciliation is that the sign depends on the type of uncertainty (expropriation-risk versus funding-risk), the horizon and reversibility of the shock, firm free cash flow, and the strength of country institutions — with country-level predation risk favouring disgorgement and acute funding shocks favouring conservation. The firm-level precautionary motive documented in financial-flexibility-and-payout is the through-line, and CEO-level channels show that who decides matters alongside where. What is not yet settled is a unified model that predicts the sign ex ante from observable features of the shock and the institutional setting.
